1926 Art Deco façade on quai du Louvre
source_passage: In 1926 Franz Jourdain and Henri Sauvage built the fagade on the quai du Louvre, one of the best examples of Art Deco in Paris

script_body: On 24 August 1572, at the stroke of midnight, began one of the bloodiest pages in French history: the massacre of Saint-Bartholomew, ordered by Charles IX but instigated by his mother Catherine de Medici, during which 3,000 Protestants perished. Of the three bells that signalled the onset of the carnage — Marie, Germain and Vincent — only Marie has survived. It dates from 1527 and is one of the oldest bells in Paris. Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois was the royal parish church, just opposite the Louvre, and the royal pew can still be seen inside.
physical_cues: the royal pew can still be seen inside
source_passage: On 24 August 1572, at the stroke of midnight, began one of the bloodiest pages in French history: the massacre of Saint-Bartholomew

script_body: When Catherine de Medici was told by her astrologer, Ruggieri, that she would die 'by Saint-Germain,' she moved out of the Palais des Tuileries so as to attend mass elsewhere, and settled in the Hôtel de Soissons. She never returned to her residence at Saint-Germain-en-Laye either. But there is no escaping one's destiny: while in Blois in the Loire Valley some 16 years later, she took ill, never to recover. A young priest was called to her bedside on 15 January 1589. The Queen asked his name: 'Julien de Saint-Germain,' replied the holy stranger.
key_claims: Died 15 Jan 1589 attended by priest named Saint-Germain
source_passage: A young priest was called to her bedside on 15 January 1589... 'Julien de Saint-Germain,' replied the holy stranger

script_body: The Galerie Véro-Dodat, entered through no. 19 rue J.J. Rousseau, carries you nearly two centuries back. Its beautiful glass ceiling, black-and-white chequered floor, mahogany panelling, and brass framings served as backdrop to the promenade of fair ladies in crinolines and gentlemen in tail-coats when it opened in 1826. The arcade's gas lights created quite a sensation and property prices rocketed. But somehow, Messieurs Vérot and Dodat — the two pork butchers who had built it — went bankrupt. In the late 1830s the celebrated actress Rachel moved to the 3rd floor of no. 38. The ground floor was occupied by the satirical paper Charivari, to which Daumier contributed his cartoons, and where the word 'Impressionist' was first coined by the journalist Leroy.
physical_cues: beautiful glass ceiling, black-and-white chequered floor, mahogany panelling
key_claims: Built by two pork butchers who went bankrupt
source_passage: The arcade's gas lights created quite a sensation and prices of property rocketed. But somehow, Messieurs Verot and Dodat, the two charcutiers who had built the arcade, went bankrupt

script_body: The Banque de France, founded in 1800 on Napoleon's initiative, moved in 1812 to the sumptuous Hôtel de la Vrillière, built by Mansart in 1635 for the Marquis de la Vrillière. In 1713 the Comte de Toulouse — the legitimized son of Louis XIV and Madame de Montespan — bought it and totally transformed it, adding the stunning Galerie Dorée of approximately 40 metres, which many prefer to the one in Versailles. Unfortunately, this magnificent example of French early 18th-century interior decoration is rarely open to the public.
key_claims: Moved to Hôtel de la Vrillière 1812
source_passage: the stunning 50-metre long Galerie Dorée, which many prefer to the one in Versailles

script_body: François d'Aubusson, Maréchal and Duc de La Feuillade, idolized Louis XIV so much that he put up a statue at his own expense on his own property. The statue was all covered with gold, with a disproportionately large head decorated with a laurel wreath. At the King's feet, four chained women dramatically embodied his trampled enemies — Spain, Holland, Germany and Franche-Comté. La Feuillade then called upon Jules Hardouin-Mansart to create a setting worthy of his idol: the result was the elegant Place des Victoires. La Feuillade, by then the laughing stock of Paris, is said to have relieved the King when he finally gave up the ghost. The statue was melted down during the Revolution; the current one by Bosio shows the Sun King on a horse, dressed as a Roman emperor — but keeping his wig.
key_claims: La Feuillade built golden statue at own expense
Current statue by Bosio keeps the wig
source_passage: La Feuillade, by then the laughing stock of Paris, is said to have relieved the King when he finally gave up the ghost

script_body: During Napoleon's Consulate, a statue to General Desaix — the hero of the battle of Marengo — stood in Place des Victoires, representing the hero in his natural attire, emulating the heroes of ancient times. But the population of Paris was shocked by such indecent exposure and a fence was soon set up around the General to keep him out of view. In 1976, designer Kenzo signalled the rejuvenation of the area, its transformation into a stronghold of contemporary créateurs as opposed to traditional couturiers.
key_claims: Naked Desaix statue shocked Paris, fenced off
source_passage: the population of Paris was shocked by such indecent exposure and a fence was soon set up around the General to keep him out of view

script_body: When the palace was built for Richelieu it was known as le Palais-Cardinal. He bequeathed it to Louis XIII, and after the latter's death the royal family moved in. To facilitate Mazarin's rendezvous with Anne of Austria, a door was fitted into the palace wall — which proved handy during the Fronde in 1650, when the Queen and her two sons, the future Louis XIV and Philippe d'Orléans, escaped to Saint-Germain-en-Laye. The Regent Philippe d'Orléans later made the Palais-Royal notorious for his 'soupers' — veritable bacchanalia. His grandson Philippe, deep in debt, built the arcades and shops, turning it into a profitable business with gambling houses and brothels. 'Cousin,' said Louis XVI disdainfully, 'you have turned shop-keeper.' Philippe would have his revenge: in 1793, as Philippe Égalité, he voted for the death of his royal cousin. The guillotine took charge of him too, a few months later.
key_claims: Mazarin's secret door for Anne of Austria
Philippe Égalité voted for Louis XVI's death then guillotined
source_passage: Cousin, he said disdainfully, you have turned shop-keeper and no doubt we shall see you only on Sundays

script_body: Among the shops of the newly converted Palais-Royal was a cutlery establishment at no. 177 Galerie de Valois, which belonged to Monsieur Badin. Here on 13 July 1793, Charlotte Corday bought the knife with which she stabbed Marat in his bathtub the same day.
key_claims: Cutlery shop at 177 Galerie de Valois
Stabbed Marat in bathtub same day
source_passage: Here on 13 July 1793 Charlotte Corday bought the knife with which she stabbed Marat in his bathtub the same day

script_body: By the time Colette was living at 9 rue de Beaujolais and Jean Cocteau at 36 rue de Montpensier, the Palais-Royal had assumed its present aspect of outdated serenity. Colette described its nameless, silent citizens who followed a code of mysterious mutual courtesy: the elderly lady leaning on her stick, the gentleman cultivating cacti on his window sill. Cocteau, more than just a neighbour, was a friend and admirer who called Colette 'an ink fountain.' He described the gardens as 'La campagne en plein centre de Paris.'
key_claims: Cocteau called Colette an ink fountain
source_passage: Colette was living at 9 rue de Beaujolais, and Jean Cocteau at 36 rue de Montpensier

script_body: The Comédie-Française was built between 1786 and 1790 by Victor Louis, the architect of the famous theatre of Bordeaux. The Comédiens-Français took over in 1799, with an inauguration of Le Cid and L'École des Maris, starring the great Talma and the adulated Mlle Mars. In the 17th century, another theatre had stood nearby on the corner of rue de Valois and rue Saint-Honoré, built by Richelieu and named Le Petit Cardinal. It was here that at 10 pm on 17 February 1673, Molière was acting the part of Argan in Le Malade Imaginaire when he collapsed during the performance and died later that evening at home.
key_claims: Molière collapsed 17 Feb 1673 in Le Malade Imaginaire
Died later that evening at home
source_passage: at 10 pm on 17 February 1673 Moliére was acting the part of Argan, le Malade Imaginaire, when he collapsed on the stage

script_body: At no. 228 rue de Rivoli is the discreet entrance to the celebrated Meurice, where Thackeray and Dickens once stayed and where penniless George Orwell was widely believed to have worked to the bone as a plongeur — 'the slave of the slave' — as described in Down and Out in London and Paris. The hotel, which he omits to name, is 'a vast, grandiose place with a classical façade, and at one side a little, dark doorway like a rat hole, which was the service entrance.' The kitchens were 'a stifling low-ceilinged inferno of a cellar, red-lit from the fires, and deafening with oaths and clanging of pots and pans.' Only a double door separated the squalid scullery from the posh dining-room.
key_claims: Orwell widely believed to have worked as plongeur here
Down and Out in London and Paris descriptions
source_passage: penniless Orwell was worked to the bone as a plongeur, the slave of the slave, as we learn in Down and Out in London and Paris

script_body: During the Second World War, the German High Command of the Paris garrison took up residence at the lavish Meurice.
key_claims: German High Command Paris garrison at Le Meurice WWII
source_passage: the German High Command of the Paris garrison who, during the last war, took up residence at the lavish Meurice

script_body: Saint-Roch being the fashionable church of Paris, many illustrious Parisians were buried here — Pierre Corneille, Diderot, d'Holbach, André Le Nôtre, and Marie-Anne de Bourbon, the daughter of Louis XIV and his first mistress Louise de la Vallière. The funeral of the great Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux, was also celebrated here. The financier John Law donated 100,000 pounds towards the church's completion — not for spiritual motivation, but to be appointed contrôleur général. To that end he also converted to Catholicism, and it was at Saint-Roch that he received his first Holy Communion.
key_claims: Corneille Diderot Le Nôtre buried here
Law converted to Catholicism at Saint-Roch
source_passage: the financier Law had not donated 100,000 pounds towards its completion, not for any spiritual motivation, but so as to be appointed contréleur général

script_body: Place Vendôme sums up the switchback history of 19th-century France in a single column. Girardon's original equestrian statue of the Sun King was disposed of during the Revolution. Napoleon's Colonne d'Austerlitz replaced it in 1810. With the Restoration, it was swapped for an equestrian Henri IV, le Vert Galant. When the bourgeois Louis-Philippe took the throne, the Vert Galant was dispatched to the Pont-Neuf and a Napoleon in a frock coat was set up instead — which his nephew Napoleon III later substituted with an imperial Napoleon as a Roman Caesar. In 1871 the Commune, led by the painter Courbet, toppled the column to the sound of the Marseillaise as thousands of patriots cheered. The Emperor regained his lofty position the following year when the bourgeois National Assembly sent him back to the top. He has been dominating this mecca of luxury ever since.
key_claims: Girardon's Louis XIV statue melted in Revolution
Commune toppled it 1871 led by Courbet
source_passage: thousands of patriots struck up the Marsaillaise and le Chant de la Patrie, to the sound of the triumphant fanfare, as the monument came tumbling down

script_body: Passage des Panoramas was the first place in Paris to be gaslit, in 1817 — a dazzling novelty that drew the fashionable set to promenade here. The passage took its name from two circular Panoramas installed at the site: vast painted canvases that transported spectators to bloody battlefields or peaceful foreign lands. The concept had been invented and patented by the Irish-born painter Robert Barker in 1787, and the Paris installations became the dernier cri. The passage also housed the elegant Café Véron and the pastry shop Félix, making it one of the highlights of early 19th-century Paris.
source_passage: Passage des Panoramas was one of the highlights of Paris in the last century, the first place in the city to be gaslit, in 1817

script_body: At no. 7 Boulevard Montmartre, the Théâtre des Variétés still stands — the stage where Hortense Schneider created a sensation with Offenbach's La Grande Duchesse de Gérolstein in 1867. The premiere coincided with the Universal Exposition, and the audience included Napoleon III, the Prince of Wales, the Emperor of Russia, and Bismarck. Schneider's box became known as 'the passage of princes.' Next door at no. 9, the Café des Variétés had been a stronghold of Parisian literati until 1870.
physical_cues: Théâtre des Variétés still stands at no. 7 Boulevard Montmartre
key_claims: Hortense Schneider in Offenbach's La Grande Duchesse 1867
source_passage: Le Théatre des Variétés, where Hortense Schneider created a sensation with Offenbach's La Grande Duchesse in 1867, still stands

script_body: The Paris Stock Exchange stands on the site of the convent of Les Filles de Saint-Thomas, which was closed during the Revolution. In the nascent age of capitalism, Napoleon had the convent razed and replaced it with this shrine to commerce, designed to emulate a Greek temple. For nearly two centuries it served as the nerve centre of French finance — though women were barred from entering until 1967, when Article XI prohibiting their admittance was finally repealed.
physical_cues: Stock Exchange building in Greek temple style dominates the square
source_passage: The Paris Stock Exchange stands in its centre, on the site of the convent of Les Filles de Saint-Thomas, which was closed down during the Revolution

script_body: The painting above the high altar of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires tells a story of royal gratitude. It shows the Holy Virgin seated on a cloud, with Louis XIII at her feet presenting a plan of the church — his thanks for divine help defeating his enemies. To the King's right, a man surrenders the keys of the defeated town of La Rochelle, visible in the background. To his left stands Richelieu, whose initiative it was to eliminate the Huguenots and who obtained their surrender at La Rochelle in 1628. The illustrious architect of the Invalides, Libéral Bruant, collaborated in the construction of this pilgrimage church.
physical_cues: painting above the high altar showing Louis XIII presenting church plan
source_passage: The painting above the high altar shows the Holy Virgin seated on a cloud: at her feet is Louis XIII presenting her with a plan of the church

script_body: Among the famous Parisians buried at Notre-Dame-des-Victoires was Louis XIV's court composer Lully, whose funeral monument can still be seen between two side chapels. But the church itself had a turbulent afterlife: it was looted and wrecked during the Revolution, then found an unlikely second use as the Paris stock exchange between 1796 and 1809, before the Bourse moved to its purpose-built temple on Place de la Bourse.
physical_cues: Lully's funeral monument between two side chapels
source_passage: Among famous Parisians who were buried here was Louis XIV's musician Lully. The church was looted and wrecked during the Revolution, then found use as the Paris stock exchange between 1796 and 1809

script_body: The Bibliothèque Nationale traces its origins to Charles V in the 14th century, when the king concentrated his ancestors' manuscripts in a tower of the Louvre. The collection was scattered during the Hundred Years' War but gathered again in the 16th century by Louis XII and especially by the humanistic François I. Over the centuries it grew relentlessly — swollen first by the Revolution, when a prodigious flow of books confiscated from the aristocracy and religious institutions poured in, and then by the 19th-century explosion of printing. By the late 20th century the institution held over 12 million books, 6 million engravings, 800,000 coins and medals, and 400,000 records.
source_passage: This monumental institution was initiated by Charles V in the 14th century, when he concentrated his ancestors' manuscripts in the tower of the Louvre

script_body: In 1643, Cardinal Mazarin rented a property at 8 rue des Petits-Champs — the Hôtel Tubeuf — to keep close to Richelieu's Palais-Royal. Within two years he had acquired all the land extending north to the present rue Colbert, including a second mansion. He commissioned François Mansart to build a gallery between the two mansions to house his art collection, and then a separate wing for his library of 40,000 volumes — the most impressive in Europe. Mazarin had sent emissaries to every court and kingdom with orders to buy every book unavailable in Paris, acquiring between 30,000 and 35,000 volumes in less than ten years.
source_passage: In 1643 Mazarin rented a property at 8 rue des Petits-Champs, the Hétel Tubeuf

script_body: Two hidden arcades lie side by side here — the highlight of the 2nd arrondissement. The Galerie Vivienne, with its tasteful, arty boutiques and good bookshops, has a charming, antiquated feel. Next door, the Galerie Colbert has been renovated into a more formal, classical compound in true French style, enhanced by its pale pink stone. Both offer an ideal refuge on a wet day — a glimpse of the covered-passage culture that once defined Parisian shopping.
physical_cues: Galerie Vivienne with arty boutiques and bookshops
Galerie Colbert with pale pink stone
source_passage: On your left are two delightful hidden arcades - the highlight of the 2nd arrondissement - Galeries Vivienne and Colbert

script_body: Square Louvois stands on the site of Paris's ninth opera house. On 13 February 1820, the Duc de Berry — younger son of the future Charles X — was stabbed at the royal doorway of the theatre by a Bonapartist saddler named Louvel, as part of a scheme to rid France of the House of Bourbon. The Duke died the following day. Louvel was caught and guillotined before he could do more harm, and the King ordered the opera house razed to obliterate the scene of the crime. Today a graceful fountain by Visconti stands in its place, its allegorical figures representing the four biggest rivers of France that bear feminine names — which explains why the Rhône is not among them.
physical_cues: Visconti fountain with allegorical river figures
source_passage: On 13 February 1820, the Duc de Berry, eldest son of the future Charles X, was assassinated at the royal doorway of the theatre

script_body: Lully actually lived nearby, in the corner house at nos. 45 rue des Petits-Champs and 47 rue Sainte-Anne. Its listed façade is decorated with musical instruments and masks of Bacchantes and satyrs — a fitting home for the composer who dominated French music under Louis XIV. The street names around Square Louvois — Cherubini, Rameau and Lully — are the only reminders of the neighbourhood's lyrical past.
physical_cues: listed façade with musical instruments and masks at 45 rue des Petits-Champs / 47 rue Sainte-Anne
source_passage: Lully actually lived near by, in the corner house at n°s 45 rue des Petits-Champs and 47 rue Sainte-Anne

script_body: At no. 6 rue Rameau, at the beginning of the 19th century, lived the idolized tenor Adolphe Nourrit, who premiered all the masterpieces of his time — the works of Rossini and Meyerbeer among them. During a performance of Halévy's La Juive in Marseille, he suffered a vocal crisis that ended his career. Devastated, he threw himself from a window in Naples in 1839. He was only 37.
source_passage: the idolized tenor Adolphe Nourrit, who premiered all the masterpieces of the time, lived at n° 6 rue Rameau

script_body: Nearby rue Chabanais, opened in 1776, was famous above all for the internationally renowned brothel at no. 12, which from 1878 to 1946 catered to the exclusive clientele of the Jockey Club on Boulevard des Italiens. Most of the crowned heads of Europe frequented this impeccably tasteful establishment, as did ministers and government leaders of the Third Republic. Their visits were discreetly described on official timetables as 'visit to the President of the Sénat.' The splendid furniture was dispersed at auction at Drouot on 8 May 1951.
physical_cues: 18th-century mansions with wrought-iron decorations on rue Chabanais
source_passage: rue Chabanais was famous first and foremost for its internationally renowned brothel at n° 12, which from 1878 to 1946 catered to the exclusive clientele

script_body: Passage de Choiseul, built in 1825, was once imbued with a rich cultural life. At no. 23 stood a publishing house that brought the Parnasse poets to the world — Sully Prudhomme, Leconte de Lisle, Heredia and François Coppée — followed from 1864 by Paul Verlaine. A few years later Anatole France worked here as editor for roughly a decade. At no. 73, the stage door to the winter Bouffes Parisiens still stands, where Jacques Offenbach, then director of the theatre, could be seen walking through during the winter seasons of 1855 to 1863.
physical_cues: stage door to winter Bouffes Parisiens at no. 73
source_passage: Until 1965 n° 23 was the site of a publishing house which published the works of the Parnasse poets

script_body: In the celebrated Drouant restaurant on the corner of 18 rue Gaillon, the Goncourt Prize — the most prestigious of French literary prizes — is awarded every third Monday of November. Charles Drouant came up to Paris from Alsace in 1880, one of many compatriots torn by the loss of their region to the Germans. His restaurant soon attracted artists and writers with its fresh oysters from Brittany, and Alphonse and Léon Daudet, Rodin, Renoir, and Edmond de Goncourt became regulars. On 10 December 1919, Léon Daudet brought Proust the letter announcing he had won the prize for À l'ombre des Jeunes Filles en fleurs — though by a narrow margin of six votes to four over Dorgelès's war novel Les Croix de Bois.
physical_cues: Drouant restaurant on corner of rue Gaillon
source_passage: In the celebrated Drouant restaurant on the comer of 18 rue Gaillon, the Goncourt Prize, the most prestigious of French literary prizes, is awarded every third Monday of November

script_body: At no. 5 rue Daunou, the red neon sign of Harry's Bar still beckons from a quiet, deserted street. This was a favourite haunt of Hemingway, whose photograph hangs on the wall, and of his friend Fitzgerald, who would drop in from the Ritz just round the corner. Opened in 1911, Harry's New York Bar was the heart of American expatriate Paris in the 1920s — and the birthplace of the Bloody Mary cocktail, mixed here by bartender Fernand Petiot in 1921.
physical_cues: red neon sign of Harry's Bar
source_passage: At n° 5 the red neon sign of Harry's Bar still stands out in the night in the otherwise dark, deserted street

script_body: Rue de la Paix was once the site of the beautiful convent of the Capucines, closed during the Revolution and converted into a theatre. A popular funfair was held in its gardens and the famous Franconi moved his circus there. In 1806, Napoleon razed everything to make room for a glorious thoroughfare to honour his name, entrusting the project to his architects Percier and Fontaine. After his defeat in 1814, however, the street was renamed rue de la Paix to commemorate the Peace of Amiens.
source_passage: once the site of the church of the beautiful convent of the Capucines. The convent was closed down during the Revolution

script_body: At no. 7 was the house of Charles Frederick Worth, rightly claimed to be the first haute couture designer, who raised dressmaking from craft to art. When Worth arrived from England in 1845, aged 20, he had just 117 francs in his pocket and knew not a word of French. He had served seven years apprenticed to the drapers Swan and Edgar, and after 12 years of hard work in Paris opened his own house on rue de la Paix in 1858. His timing was perfect: this was the heyday of the glamorous Second Empire, where multitudes of social upstarts, ready to squander unlimited sums, accepted Worth's tyranny because they could not claim to be his social betters. The reign of the haute couture designer thus began.
source_passage: At n° 7 was the house of Charles Worth, rightly claimed to be the first haute couture designer

script_body: The head office of Cartier is still at no. 13 rue de la Paix. The house was founded in 1847 by Louis-François Cartier, who until then had been working for another famous jeweller, Adolphe Picard. He first set up shop near the Palais-Royal, then moved to the fashionable Boulevard des Italiens, where his customers included the Empress Eugénie and Napoleon III's cousin, la Princesse Mathilde. In 1899 his grandson Louis moved to rue de la Paix, by then the centre of luxury of the capital. Cartier's international clientele included Edward VII of England, Alfonso XIII of Spain, and the Duchess of Windsor.
physical_cues: Cartier head office at no. 13 rue de la Paix
source_passage: The head office of the jeweller Cartier is still at n° 13 rue de la Paix. The house was founded in 1847 by Louis Ferdinand Cartier

script_body: In 1892, the prosperous banker Paquin set up his wife at no. 5 rue de la Paix. Madame Jeanne Paquin was the first major woman couturier and also the first woman in fashion to be awarded the Légion d'honneur, in 1913. A prominent public figure, she chaired the fashion section of the 1900 Universal Exhibition. At its peak, 2,700 employees worked for her establishment, which was located above Robert's chemist shop — opened in 1820 by Dr Roberts, chemist and surgeon to the British Embassy, and now the sole reminder of the street's former glories among the travel agencies.
physical_cues: Robert's chemist shop still standing on rue de la Paix
key_claims: First woman in fashion Légion d'honneur 1913
source_passage: Madame Paquin was the first woman designer and also the first woman to be awarded the Légion d'honneur in 1913

script_body: For nearly two centuries, the Paris stock exchange, La Bourse, has stood imposingly in the heart of the 2nd arrondissement, marking it as the financial centre of the capital. Napoleon commissioned architect Alexandre-Théodore Brongniart to endow the city with a new temple of finance, modeled on Roman temples — specifically the Temple of Vespasian and the Maison Carrée in Nîmes. Napoleon was not to see the completed monument: it was inaugurated in 1826, eleven years after his downfall. Originally, the Tribunal of Trade was also located here, but was transferred to Boulevard du Palais on Île de la Cité during the Second Empire.
key_claims: Tribunal of Trade moved during Second Empire
source_passage: Napoleon commissioned his architect Brongniart to endow the city with a new temple of finance, emulating those of ancient Greece

script_body: In 1670, Louis XIV — fortified by his military victories — did away with the city walls and laid out tree-lined promenades in their place, emulating the Cour-la-Reine planted by his grandmother Marie de Medici along the Seine. These Grands Boulevards — the word comes from the German 'Bollwerk,' meaning the surface of a rampart — ran in a circular arc from the Madeleine to the Bastille, a long stretch that marked the northern boundary of Paris. By the 19th century they had become the playground of the privileged classes and the heart of the modern capital, symbolized by the first omnibus line which plied along them.
source_passage: In 1676 Louis XIV, fortified by his military victories, did away with the walls and laid out a tree-lined promenade instead

script_body: The Porte Saint-Denis has been the gateway to the city since the reign of Charles V in the 14th century. In 1672, Louis XIV — confident that Paris no longer needed to be defended after his spectacular victories — had architect François Blondel replace the medieval gate, a crenellated construction complete with towers and drawbridge, with the present triumphal arch for the sole purpose of glorifying his person. Since Roman days, this had been the route by which travelers entered and left the capital along rue Saint-Denis, which led to the villages of Saint-Denis and Pontoise, and on to Rouen. From the 8th century it became the royal highway through which the kings and queens of France entered solemnly 'the good city of Paris' on their way to Notre-Dame — a tradition maintained for over a thousand years, right up to the coronation of Charles X in 1827.
physical_cues: Look up at the triumphal arch spanning the boulevard
source_passage: In 1672, Louis XIV, confident that the city no longer needed to be defended after his spectacular victories, had Blondel replace the 14th-century gate

script_body: Even those traveling to their deaths found solace on rue Saint-Denis. The tumbril carrying condemned prisoners from the prison of the Grand-Châtelet to the gallows of Montfaucon would pause at the convent of the Filles-Dieu to let them kiss the wooden cross. The convent's inmates — reformed prostitutes — would offer holy water, three morsels of bread and a glass of wine, and could even save their necks by consenting to marry them. It is said that one prisoner, offered rescue by a generous yet hideously ugly 'daughter of God,' urged the hangman to proceed with his task and deliver him from a still worse fate.
source_passage: The tumbril carrying them from the prison of the Grand-Chatelet would pause to allow them to kiss the wooden cross of the convent of the Filles-Dieu

script_body: The Hôpital de la Trinité once extended between 164 and 142 rue Saint-Denis, set up originally for travelers unable to enter the city after curfew. In 1402, the Confrérie de la Passion rented a hall here and staged religious 'mysteries' telling the life of Jesus — making this the first permanent, officially authorized theatrical venue in Paris and the birthplace of Parisian theatre. So popular were these performances that the hospital became the capital's centre of entertainment. In the 16th century it became an orphanage for boys and girls known as 'Les Enfants Bleus' for their blue uniforms, and the children were taught crafts from a young age, generating a flourishing arts-and-crafts tradition in the area. At n°142 stands the Fontaine Greneta, built in 1502 — one of the oldest fountain sites in Paris.
physical_cues: Look for the Passage de la Trinité entrance at n°164
key_claims: 1402 Confrérie de la Passion staged mysteries
source_passage: In 1402 the Confréres de la Passion were let a hall here and began to produce religious 'mysteries'

corrections.corrected_text: orphanage for boys and girls (100 boys, 36 girls)

script_body: At 145 rue Saint-Denis stands the Passage du Grand-Cerf, where before the Revolution a famous hostelry called 'the big stag' was situated. This was the Paris terminal of the royal mail-coach service to the north and east — the Messageries Royales connecting Paris with Alsace, Champagne and Flanders. The arcade has been recently renovated and now reflects the elegance of a newly gentrified Paris, its soaring glass ceiling making it one of the tallest covered passages in the city.
physical_cues: Look up at the tall glass-roofed arcade
source_passage: le Passage du Grand-Cerf where a famous hostelry by the same name ('the big hart') was situated before the Revolution

sources_consulted: Multiple Paris passage guides and historical references

script_body: At 20 rue Étienne-Marcel stands Paris's only surviving medieval military tower. In 1270, Robert II d'Artois, nephew of Saint Louis, built a hôtel here, which later passed to the House of Bourgogne. After the assassination of his cousin Louis, Duc d'Orléans, by his men in 1407, Jean sans Peur, Duc de Bourgogne, began constructing a defence tower within the walls of his property between 1409 and 1411. Knowing he had many foes, he slept on the topmost floor, sandwiched between his squire below and crossbowmen on the crenellated roof. A spiral staircase leads to his room, its vault carved with intertwined branches of oak, hawthorn and hops — emblems of the Burgundian dynasty. Despite these precautions, destiny caught up with him twelve years later: he was killed on the bridge of Montereau by Tanguy du Châtel, head of the Armagnacs, the supporters of his murdered cousin.
physical_cues: Look for the medieval tower at n°20
The carved oak, hawthorn and hops vault is visible at the top of the spiral staircase
source_passage: Jean sans Peur, Duc de Bourgogne, was back in Paris after a year's absence following the assassination by his men of his cousin, Philippe Duc d'Orléans

corrections.original_text: oak tree symbolizing the House of Bourgogne
corrections.corrected_text: oak, hawthorn and hops — three family emblems

script_body: Just across the street at n°29 stood the Théâtre de l'Hôtel de Bourgogne, the first permanent theatre of Paris. In 1548, the Confrérie de la Passion took possession of this site, vacated by François I. Through wily lobbying, the resident Comédiens du Roi enjoyed Louis XIV's patronage and produced Racine's work. In 1680, Louis XIV ordered two rival troupes to merge — creating the Comédie-Française — and the Italian troupe took over, delighting Parisians with Harlequin, Colombine and Scaramouche. When they derided Madame de Maintenon as 'La Fausse Prude' in 1697, she had the theatre shut down. The fun-loving Regent brought them back in 1716, and they entertained audiences with Marivaux's light-hearted comedies until 1783, when they moved to new premises near the Boulevard des Italiens — named after them.
key_claims: 1548 Confrérie de la Passion moved here
source_passage: In 1548 the Confréres de la Passion were expelled from the Hopital de la Trinité and took possession of this site

script_body: Rue Montorgueil was the fish section of the great market of Les Halles and the central oyster market of Paris until 1866. Since the fresh sea catch from the north arrived here, the street was lined with fish stalls and the sales office of the oyster trade from Étretat and Dieppe operated from n°61/63. Rue Montorgueil was also a gourmet's mecca: the restaurant Le Rocher de Cancale at n°59 was, in Balzac's estimation, 'the meeting place of the best society of Paris and the establishment which best honours French cuisine.' All the heroes of La Comédie Humaine dined there, alongside Dumas père, Eugène Sue and Théophile Gautier. The building still stands with the name engraved on its shabby facade.
physical_cues: Look for the name 'Rocher de Cancale' engraved on the facade near n°59
key_claims: Le Rocher de Cancale at n°59
source_passage: this became the fish section of the market of Les Halles and also the central oyster market of Paris until 1866

script_body: It was in Madame Gourdan's establishment on what is now rue Montorgueil that the notorious pimp Jean du Barry discovered the enticing Jeanne Bécu, known by her trade name Mademoiselle Lange. Having set her up as a courtesan, he introduced her to the Duc de Richelieu, who facilitated her presentation to Louis XV. A true professional, Jeanne introduced the licentious monarch to unsuspected pleasures, all the more appreciated since his predecessor, the Pompadour, had long lost her appetite. To make her socially acceptable, Jean du Barry married her off to his brother, Comte Guillaume, while the new Comtesse du Barry became the last of France's royal favourites. Outside the court, the people were infuriated by her prodigal spending. When the time came for revenge, a vindictive nation sent for her at her retreat in Louveciennes and dispatched her to the guillotine.
key_claims: Jean du Barry discovered Jeanne Bécu
Married to Comte Guillaume du Barry
source_passage: it was in Madame Gourdan's glamorous establishment on rue de la Comtesse d'Artois (now rue Montorgueil), that the notorious pimp Jean du Barry discovered the enticing Jeanne Bécu

disputes.claim: How du Barry met Bécu at Gourdan's
disputes.note: Exact circumstances contested across sources; core narrative preserved

script_body: You are standing in the one-time realm of the underworld — the notorious Cour des Miracles, immortalized in Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris. Between the 15th and 17th centuries, the destitute organized into fearsome bands with their own language and laws. By day they spilled into the streets as 'blind' or 'maimed' beggars, preying upon passers-by. By night they vanished into dead-end alleys where they laid aside their crutches and 'miraculously' recovered their eyesight and missing limbs. Hugo described it as 'a gutter of vice and beggary, of vagrancy that spills over into the streets of the capital.' In 1667, Louis XIV ordered his police lieutenant Nicolas de La Reynie to clean up this hotbed of banditry. The occupants put up heroic resistance; once defeated, many ended up in the galleys of the king's fleet. The Egyptian-themed sculptures on Place du Caire commemorate Napoleon's campaigns and the Egyptomania that ensued.
physical_cues: Look for the Egyptian sphinx and lotus-column relief on the facade at 2 Place du Caire
key_claims: Victor Hugo immortalized Cour des Miracles
source_passage: a gutter of vice and beggary, of vagrancy that spills over into the streets of the capital

script_body: Of all the inhabitants of rue de Cléry, Jeanne Poisson — born roughly on the site of the present n°29 — was destined for the most glorious future. After her father François Poisson fled France, she was raised by the Farmer General Le Normant de Tournehem. When she was 23, she won the heart of Louis XV at a masked ball and became the celebrated Marquise de Pompadour, to the indignation of the court and its scandalized ladies.
key_claims: Jeanne Poisson born at n°29 rue de Cléry
Raised by Le Normant de Tournehem
source_passage: Born to an unknown father, roughly on the site of the present n° 29, she was educated by the Farmer General Le Norman de Tournehem

corrections.corrected_text: Legal father was François Poisson (biological paternity suspected of Tournehem)

entities: Farmer General Le Normant de Tournehem

script_body: Towards the end of his life, Pierre Corneille lived on rue de Cléry. After the death of his patron, the Duc de Guise, he had to vacate his apartment in the Marais. He solicited the King for lodging in the Louvre, taking the trouble to couch his request in rhyme, but the King turned a deaf ear — a deplorable attitude, as most of those granted accommodation there were base courtiers and parasites. Of all the plays he wrote on rue de Cléry, Psyché alone proved a success — written to the music of Lully, in collaboration with Quinault and Molière, it sealed Corneille's friendship with the latter. But Louis XIV, paired with the bigoted Madame de Maintenon, cut off altogether the pension of the playwright who had given him so much pleasure. On 1 October 1684, Pierre Corneille died a pauper on rue d'Argenteuil. Four days later, Psyché was taken up again, so great was its success.
key_claims: Corneille lived on rue de Cléry
source_passage: Of all those he wrote on rue de Cléry, Psyché alone proved a success. Written to the music of Lully, in collaboration with Quinault and Moliére

corrections.corrected_text: Four days later (died Oct 1, revived Oct 5)

script_body: In April 1874, the first Impressionist exhibition took place right here at 35 Boulevard des Capucines. The photographer Nadar lent his painter friends his studio for the occasion. The show was organized by the Société anonyme des artistes peintres, sculpteurs et graveurs — a joint-stock company the artists formed themselves. The press was less than sympathetic, describing the works as the product of 'hoaxers' or 'lunatics' and 'mental derangement.' It was all too much for the bourgeoisie of the nascent Third Republic — yet this exhibition would change the course of art history forever.
physical_cues: The building at n°35 marks where Nadar's studio once stood
key_claims: Organized by Société anonyme des artistes
source_passage: In 1874 the first Impressionist exhibition took place at 35 Boulevard des Capucines within the framework of the Salon des Indépendants

corrections.original_text: within the framework of the Salon des Indépendants
corrections.corrected_text: organized by the Société anonyme des artistes peintres, sculpteurs et graveurs (Salon des Indépendants not founded until 1884)

script_body: Place de Louvois was the site of the Opera House of Paris during the Restoration, and the scene of one of its darkest nights. On 13 February 1820, the Duc de Berry — heir to the throne — was assassinated here during a performance of the Carnival of Venice. The King ordered the theatre razed to the ground so as to eradicate the memory of the evil deed, which provided the congested arrondissement with its only open-air garden — the pleasant square you see today.
physical_cues: The 1844 Visconti fountain in the centre of the square marks where the opera house once stood
key_claims: Site of Opera House during Restoration
source_passage: the scene of the assassination of the Duc de Berry, heir to the throne, on 13 February 1820, during a performance of the Carnival of Venice

script_body: On 31 July 1914 — the eve of the Great War — Jean Jaurès, founder of the socialist paper L'Humanité, was having an animated dinner with fellow journalists by an open window at the Café du Croissant. Raoul Villain, a 29-year-old nationalist standing outside, drew the curtain, aimed and fired twice. Jaurès was dead for having opposed the war — and became, ironically, its first French victim. His assassin was acquitted. This neighbourhood was the heart of the Paris press. Sixteen years earlier, at nearby 140 rue Montmartre, the newspaper L'Aurore had published Émile Zola's historic J'accuse on its front page — 300,000 copies hawked on the streets of Paris in defence of Alfred Dreyfus. Tried for libel, Zola fled to England. He was found suffocated in his house on 29 September 1902 — many, including his son, have always believed it was murder.
physical_cues: Inside the café you can see a copy of L'Humanité's front page announcing Jaurès's death, and his table with a blood stain that never came off
source_passage: Jean Jaurés, the founder of the socialist paper l'Humanité, was shot dead through the window of La Chope du Croissant

script_body: Rue Notre-Dame-de-Nazareth sits at the heart of one of Paris's lesser-known Jewish enclaves. When the Revolution broke out, only about 500 Jews lived in the entire capital — Charles VI had banished them in 1394. After emancipation, Jews returned in growing numbers. The synagogue was inaugurated in 1822, but faulty construction led James de Rothschild to fund the replacement you see today.
physical_cues: Look for the synagogue entrance at number 15
source_passage: Its population now is made up predominantly of North African Jews, but when its synagogue was built in the early 19th century, it was to accommodate the Ashkenazi community

script_body: The crenellated wall across the street is a surviving section of the 13th-century fortifications of the Priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. The watch-tower owes its survival to Victor Hugo, who in 1882 protested: 'Demolish the tower — no; the architect — yes!' The priory church boasts the first example of Gothic rib vaults in the capital.
physical_cues: Look across the street at the 13th-century crenellated wall
Notice the watch-tower with its pepper-box slate roof
key_claims: First Gothic rib vaults in capital
source_passage: the medieval priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and its watch-tower

script_body: The priory had a darker side. Its gaol was the scene of a savage massacre during the Hundred Years' War. Under Louis XIV, prostitutes were kept here awaiting deportation to New Orleans. In September 1719, 180 male prisoners were chained to 180 women and marched to La Rochelle for Louisiana.
physical_cues: Imagine the four corner watch-towers and 18 turrets
source_passage: It also had a gaol, the scene of a savage massacre of the Armagnacs by the Bourguignons

script_body: The priory traces its origins to the 6th century. The monks played a major role in developing this part of Paris. It all ended with the Revolution, and in 1798 the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers was granted the premises.
source_passage: Like other early Christian shrines of Paris, the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs originated in the 6th century

script_body: The monks of Saint-Martin gave France some of its most powerful churchmen — notably Cardinal de Richelieu, the mastermind behind the centralization of French royal power under Louis XIII.
source_passage: The monks of Saint-Martin played a major role and also gave the kingdom some renowned churchmen, notably the Cardinal de Richelieu

script_body: Inside the old church of Saint-Martin, the Musee National des Techniques offers one of Paris's most underrated displays. Follow humanity's technological adventure — from sundials to satellites, from steam engines to Bleriot's aircraft, with which he crossed the Channel in 1909.
physical_cues: Look for the Gothic dining hall
key_claims: Museum in old church of Saint-Martin
source_passage: On the premises is also the Musée National des Techniques

script_body: The Porte Saint-Martin stands on the ancient Roman road from Lutetia to the north. This triumphal arch was built by Louis XIV to celebrate his victories. Walk up close and see the Sun King sculpted nude as Hercules — but bewigged as always.
physical_cues: Walk up close to see Louis XIV sculpted as a nude bewigged Hercules
key_claims: Victories over Franche-Comte, Germans, Spanish, Dutch
source_passage: the Porte Saint-Martin, the triumphal arch built by Louis XIV

script_body: Rue Saint-Martin lies on the ancient Roman road from Lutetia to the north, a continuation of the Roman cardo. For centuries the Porte Saint-Martin was the ceremonial entry point to Paris.
physical_cues: Stand on rue Saint-Martin and imagine the Roman road beneath your feet
source_passage: Rue Saint-Martin lies on the ancient Roman road from Lutetia to the north and is a continuation of the Roman cardo

script_body: At number 254, the parish church of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs illustrates the evolution from Gothic to Renaissance. Its tower dates to the early 15th century, and the Renaissance portal on the south side survives.
physical_cues: Find the Renaissance portal on the south side
source_passage: Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs provides a fine example of the evolution from the Gothic to the Renaissance style

script_body: The church holds notable burials: Mademoiselle de Scudery, who died in 1701 aged 93; Guillaume de Bude, founder of the College de France. The actor Talma was baptized here.
source_passage: Among the parishioners buried here should be mentioned Mlle de Scudéry, who died in 1701 aged 94, Guillaume de Budé

script_body: At number 3 rue Volta, a medieval half-timbered house shared by a Chinese restaurant and hairstylist. For decades proclaimed the oldest house in Paris. This tiny Chinatown is the oldest Chinese community in Paris, descended from WWI immigrants.
physical_cues: Look up at the half-timbered facade at number 3
source_passage: An astonishing anachronistic sight awaits you at n° 3

script_body: The Convent of the Madelonnettes was built in 1618 to save 'fallen women.' Ninon de Lenclos was imprisoned by Anne of Austria. She protested she was 'neither a whore nor repented.' When demolished in 1865, skeletons were found under a trap-door.
physical_cues: Look for surviving convent walls at 6 rue des Fontaines-du-Temple
source_passage: The convent was built in 1618 for the purpose of saving the souls of fallen women

script_body: One of Paris's iconic green drinking fountains, donated by the English philanthropist Sir Richard Wallace in the 1870s after the Siege of Paris left the city's water supply devastated. The fountains were designed to provide free clean drinking water to all Parisians.
physical_cues: Look for the distinctive green cast-iron fountain with four caryatids
source_passage: Wallace fountain providing free drinking water

script_body: Beneath Notre-Dame's chancel, vestiges of the Pilier des Nautes were found in 1711 — a monument to Jupiter erected by the water merchants during Emperor Tiberius's reign (AD 14-37), the oldest sculpted monument in the capital.
source_passage: vestiges of a pillar-shaped monument dedicated to Jupiter, found in 1711

script_body: Between 1163 and 1330, anonymous artisans carved Notre-Dame from stone, slipping from Romanesque to Gothic yet sustaining architectural unity. Bishop Maurice de Sully initiated the project.
source_passage: Between 1163 and 1330, man's yearnings for the divine were carved into her stone

script_body: Notre-Dame hosted only two coronations, both controversial: Henry VI of England and Napoleon. Legitimate French dynasties used Reims. Henri IV's conversion to Catholicism was celebrated here in 1593 with a Te Deum, though the conversion ceremony itself took place at Saint-Denis.
source_passage: only two coronations, both controversial

script_body: In Rabelais's tale, Gargantua climbed Notre-Dame's tower and urinated on the crowd, drowning 260,418 people. The city became known as Paris — from 'par rie' (for a laugh).
source_passage: Rabelais's hero Gargantua naturally went to Notre-Dame during his visit to Paris

script_body: Philippe-Auguste confiscated Jewish possessions, using proceeds to finance Les Halles, and expelled them from France in 1182. When he invited them back 16 years later, they settled on the right bank around rue des Rosiers.
key_claims: Jews returned to rue des Rosiers
source_passage: Philippe-Auguste confiscated the Jews' possessions

script_body: The Ile Saint-Louis was originally two islands: l'Ile Notre-Dame and l'Ile aux Vaches. A 14th-century defence tower with moat divided them. In the 17th century, they were united.
source_passage: a defence tower was built on its eastern tip with a moat

script_body: The municipality grew from the corporation of water merchants who bought the strand from Louis VII. Their seal, inherited from the ancient Nautae Parisiaci, remains the coat of arms of Paris.
key_claims: Water merchants bought strand from Louis VII
source_passage: the strand was an invaluable asset to the corporation of water merchants

script_body: Etienne Marcel bought a two-storeyed house from the king in 1357, known as La Maison des Piliers. It was eventually replaced by a Renaissance building begun under Francois I.
source_passage: Etienne Marcel was the first provost to settle in a town hall

script_body: The anti-bourgeois Commune burnt down the Hotel de Ville in 1871. The Third Republic rebuilt it at once in its old style, to brush off this incident.
source_passage: The anti-bourgeois proletarian Commune burnt it down in 1871

script_body: Place de Greve served as Paris's main place of public executions. Notable executions included Cartouche, Ravaillac, and the Marquise de Brinvilliers.
source_passage: the Place de Gréve is remembered above all as the main place of public executions

script_body: On Friday 17 July 1676, Madame de Sevigne watched the Marquise de Brinvilliers carried to Place de Greve. The Marquise had poisoned her father (ten attempts) and two brothers. Sevigne wrote: 'At last, it is all over, the Brinvilliers is in the air.'
source_passage: On Friday 17 July 1676, Madame de Sévigné watched the Marquise de Brinvilliers

script_body: Place de Greve was where people gathered to seek work — 'faire la greve.' The expression now means 'to go on strike' — the opposite of its original meaning.
key_claims: Faire la greve originally meant seeking work
source_passage: The Place de Gréve was a focal site where people would gather

script_body: Place de Greve hosted the fete de la Saint-Jean on 24 June, with a 10-metre-high bonfire. Occasionally the King himself would come to light the fire, heralded by trumpets.
source_passage: the féte de la Saint-Jean on 24 June, when a 10-metre-high bonfire

script_body: Place Royale was the first open-air square in Paris. Its pink brick and white stone pavilions served as backdrop for the 1612 double wedding of Louis XIII and Elisabeth.
physical_cues: pink brick and white stone pavilions
source_passage: This was the first open-air square in Paris

script_body: Place Royale was a favourite site for duels. Richelieu banned duels in 1626. When Boutteville contravened the ruling, Richelieu had him decapitated.
physical_cues: Place des Vosges arcades and balconies
source_passage: Place Royale was also a favourite choice for duels

script_body: The Marais in its golden age was studded with magnificent hotels. Mansart, Le Vau, Le Brun, Mignard and Vouet decorated the interiors. The Duc de Richelieu sold ten Poussin paintings to buy twenty Rubens.
source_passage: great architects such as Mansart and Le Vau and painters such as Le Brun

script_body: With the court's transfer to Versailles in 1682, the Marais declined. In 1962, Malraux's rehabilitation bill passed; in 1965 the area was declared a protected zone.
source_passage: With the transfer of the court to Versailles in 1682

script_body: Rogers and Piano designed the Centre with bright piping. Parisians called them 'hippy' architects who built a 'refinery.' Yet it drew 28,000 visitors per day, beating the Eiffel Tower's 2.5 million annually.
source_passage: Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano sought to express the spirit of the time

script_body: The piazza became a focal point of street life — buskers, acrobats, mime artists, jugglers, fire-eaters, portrait painters and pickpockets recreating the medieval atmosphere of the parvis of Notre-Dame.
source_passage: Buskers, acrobats, mime artists, jugglers share this spacious square

script_body: Built in the 14th century for ammunition, the Arsenal lay along an arm of the Seine. In 1563 a gigantic explosion — heard 46 km away in Melun — blew most of it up. The Duc de Sully built a palatial residence. Louis XIV used the foundry to cast bronze statues for Versailles.
source_passage: Built in the 14th century for the manufacture of ammunition

script_body: It was while Henri IV was on his way to the Arsenal from the Louvre, on 14 May 1610, that Ravaillac jumped onto his coach and stabbed him to death.
source_passage: It was in fact while Henri IV was on his way to the Arsenal from the Louvre

script_body: The Arsenal housed the trial of Nicolas Fouquet in 1664. Despite Colbert's rigged magistrates, d'Ormesson defied the King's wish for death and voted for banishment. Louis XIV commuted it upward to life imprisonment.
source_passage: this was where the scandalous trial of Nicolas Foucquet

script_body: La Voisin's trial in 1680 at the Arsenal: women of distinction set out to eliminate those they found cumbersome. So many high-ranking names leaked that procedures were hastened to silence her.
source_passage: La Voisin's trial in 1680 was another memorable event

script_body: Charles Nodier, head of the library from 1824 to 1844, gathered the Romantic writers Hugo, Lamartine, Musset, Dumas and Sainte-Beuve.
key_claims: Hugo, Lamartine, Musset, Dumas gathered here
source_passage: Charles Nodier, the head of the library from 1824 to 1844

script_body: The Arsenal houses the apartment of Madame de Meilleraye, a unique surviving Louis XIII interior. Simon Vouet created the splendid decorations.
source_passage: The apartment of Madame de Meilleraye provides a unique example of a Louis XIII interior

script_body: The Pavillon de l'Arsenal, a 19th-century glass and steel structure, served as an art gallery and later a Samaritaine warehouse. Since 1988 it has housed exhibitions on Paris town planning.
source_passage: Across the street is the Pavillon de l'Arsenal

script_body: The Bastille functioned as a luxury prison. Voltaire completed Oedipe here. The Marquis de Sade draped his cell walls. When stormed on July 14, 1789, only seven prisoners were found.
physical_cues: Look for the fortress outline in paving stones
source_passage: Voltaire completed Oedipe; Sade draped his cell walls

script_body: Sade was transferred to the Bastille from Vincennes in 1784. He fashioned a megaphone and shouted that prisoners were being murdered. He was removed July 2, 1789 — twelve days before the storming. At the Bastille he wrote Justine.
source_passage: Sade fashioned a megaphone; transferred from Vincennes 1784

script_body: The storming became the founding myth of the Revolution, yet Necker had already planned demolition. Only seven prisoners were found — four forgers, two madmen, and a young nobleman.
key_claims: Four forgers, two madmen, one nobleman
source_passage: Necker had planned demolition; only 7 prisoners found

script_body: Mansart designed this church with a 35-metre dome that became the model for the Val-de-Grace and the Invalides. Napoleon gave the church to Protestants in 1803.
source_passage: Mansart's 35m dome became the model for Val-de-Grace and Invalides

script_body: The Visitandine convent was a fashionable retreat. Madame de La Fayette retired as Soeur Angelique. Hortense Mancini poured black ink into the holy water font.
source_passage: Madame de La Fayette as Soeur Angelique; Hortense Mancini black ink

script_body: In 1578, Quelus was stabbed eighteen times in a duel near this mansion. Henri III ordered straw on the street. The Hotel later became a centre for the Catholic League, and Henri III's assassination was plotted here.
source_passage: 1578 duel; Quelus stabbed 18 times; Henri III ordered straw

script_body: Henri IV brought 200 Italian workers to make silk, planting mulberry trees. The silkworms could not survive Parisian winters, and the project was abandoned.
source_passage: Henri IV brought 200 Italian workers; silkworms couldn't survive

script_body: The Pavillon du Roi dominates the south side. 36 houses form the ensemble. Inaugurated 1612 for the double wedding. Renamed Place des Vosges in 1800.
physical_cues: Pavillon du Roi on the south side
source_passage: Pavillon du Roi, 36 houses, inaugurated 1612, renamed 1800

script_body: On September 8, 1656, Christina of Sweden made a spectacular entry into the square after abdicating her throne two years earlier.
source_passage: Christina of Sweden's spectacular entry September 8 1656

script_body: Victor Hugo moved to 6 Place des Vosges in 1832 and lived here sixteen years. He wrote Ruy Blas and sketched Les Miserables in these rooms.
source_passage: Hugo moved here 1832, wrote Ruy Blas, sketched Les Miserables

script_body: Adele carried on an affair with Sainte-Beuve. Hugo began a liaison with Juliette Drouet. A secret back staircase allowed discreet comings and goings for fifty years.
source_passage: Adele's affair with Sainte-Beuve; Hugo's liaison with Drouet; secret staircase

script_body: Built in 1624 for gambler Mesme Gallet who lost his fortune in one night. The aged Duc de Sully installed a separate staircase so his wife's lovers could come and go.
key_claims: Sully's separate staircase for wife's lovers
source_passage: Built 1624 for gambler Gallet; Sully installed separate staircase

script_body: Voltaire was beaten by the Prince de Rohan's lackeys near the Hotel de Sully. He challenged the prince to a duel but was thrown into the Bastille instead. Upon release, he left for England — an exile that shaped his political philosophy.
physical_cues: Hotel de Sully entrance on rue Saint-Antoine
source_passage: Voltaire beaten up by Prince de Rohan

script_body: In 1606, the Comte de Vermond shot dead a rival lover on the threshold of the Hotel de Sens while Queen Margot's coach was leaving. Vermond was beheaded the next day. The Hotel de Sens is one of the oldest civilian monuments in Paris.
source_passage: Queen Margot; Vermond killed rival 1606; beheaded next day

script_body: Charpentier composed his Miserere for these acoustics. Bourdaloue was so popular ladies arrived six hours early — they had a hat named after him for his lengthy sermons.
source_passage: Charpentier's Miserere; Bourdaloue preaching; hat named after him

script_body: The Jesuits arrived in Paris in 1580. Louis XIII laid the cornerstone in 1627, and Richelieu celebrated the first mass in 1641.
source_passage: Jesuits arrived 1580; Louis XIII cornerstone 1627; Richelieu mass 1641

script_body: The Village Saint-Paul is a warren of antique courtyards. It takes its name from a 7th-century church destroyed by the Norsemen.
source_passage: Named after 7th-century church destroyed by Norsemen

script_body: Built for Diane de France, Henri II's illegitimate daughter. Lamoignon established a literary academy attracting Racine, Boileau, and Sevigne. Site of the La Brinvilliers trial.
physical_cues: Look for hunting motifs on the facade
source_passage: Built for Diane de France; Lamoignon's literary academy; La Brinvilliers trial

script_body: The only religious building by Hector Guimard, famous for his Metro entrances. He married Miss Oppenheimer, suggesting a personal Jewish connection.
physical_cues: Look at the sinuous Art Nouveau facade
source_passage: Hector Guimard Art Nouveau; only religious building he created

script_body: Rue des Rosiers is the backbone of the pletzel. At number 20 stood the Hotel des Juifs. 165 pupils were deported from a local school during the Occupation.
source_passage: Backbone of pletzel; Hotel des Juifs at no 20; 165 pupils deported

script_body: An inscription reads 'N'OUBLIEZ PAS' — Do Not Forget. It commemorates the 165 Jewish pupils deported and murdered. None survived.
physical_cues: Look for the N'OUBLIEZ PAS inscription on the school wall
source_passage: N'OUBLIEZ PAS inscription; 165 deported pupils

script_body: Beaumarchais lived here from 1776 and wrote Le Mariage de Figaro. He also set up a front company to supply arms to the American revolutionaries with Louis XVI's tacit approval.
source_passage: Beaumarchais from 1776 wrote Le Mariage de Figaro; arms for American Revolution

script_body: Named after white-robed begging friars from Marseilles in 1258. Replaced by black-gowned Guillemites, but the name stuck. Sartre commemorated the street in a poem.
source_passage: White-robed beggars from Marseilles 1258; replaced by Guillemites; Sartre poem

script_body: In September 1792, the Princesse de Lamballe was dragged from her cell and murdered by the mob. Her head was impaled on a pike and paraded before Marie-Antoinette's windows at the Temple.
source_passage: Princesse de Lamballe murdered September 1792; head displayed before Marie-Antoinette

script_body: The Centre Pompidou was conceived as a transparent cultural centre for the people — structural elements, ducts, and escalators on the exterior, leaving the interior open.
source_passage: Transparent architecture; cultural centre for the people

script_body: Parisians dubbed the Centre Pompidou 'Notre-Dame-des-Tuyaux' — Our Lady of the Pipes — capturing both outrage and grudging affection for its industrial aesthetic.
source_passage: Nicknamed Notre-Dame-des-Tuyaux

script_body: Brancusi bequeathed his entire studio to France on condition it be preserved exactly. The recreated atelier contains his tools and unfinished works. Man Ray's widow fought for the studio's preservation.
physical_cues: Look for the low modernist pavilion beside the Pompidou
key_claims: Man Ray's widow fought for preservation
source_passage: Brancusi's recreated studio; Man Ray's widow fought for studio

script_body: The Stravinsky Fountain, inaugurated in 1983, is a collaboration between Jean Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle — a joyful pop-art homage to Stravinsky's compositions.
physical_cues: Watch the mechanical sculptures spray water
source_passage: Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle pop-art fountain, 1983

corrections.corrected_text: Jean Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle

script_body: Built from 1520, Saint-Merri is one of the last Gothic churches in Paris. Its bell, cast in 1331, is the oldest in Paris.

script_body: The Val-de-Grace owes its existence to a desperate royal prayer. Anne of Austria, wife of Louis XIII, had been childless for over twenty years when she vowed to build a temple to God if granted an heir. In 1638 her prayer was answered with the birth of the future Louis XIV. Seven years later, she brought the young king to lay the cornerstone of what would become one of the finest Baroque churches in Paris.

script_body: Step inside and look up into the dome. It was the first dome fresco of its scale in Paris. The dome, designed by Lemercier after Mansart was dismissed from the project, inspired the later domes of the Pantheon and Les Invalides.

script_body: The beauty of the Val-de-Grace was recognized from the very start. Germain Brice, in the first guidebook to Paris published in 1684, wrote: 'Foreigners here must agree that things in France can be made beautiful and regular like those one goes to admire in Italy.' It was a bold claim — that Paris could rival Rome — and the Val-de-Grace was his proof.

script_body: The 5th arrondissement has the longest history of any district in mainland Paris, stretching back to the Roman occupation of Gaul. When the growing population of the Ile de la Cite spilled onto the left bank, Roman villas appeared on the slopes of Mount Leucotitius — now the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve. A north-south road, the cardo, ran along what is now rue Saint-Jacques, while a secondary cardo followed today's Boulevard Saint-Michel. By the end of the second century, this was a desirable neighbourhood of luxury — archaeological finds including marble and polychrome mosaics from rue de la Harpe attest to this. The Romans built three bath complexes: the northern ones at Cluny, the eastern ones at what is now the College de France, and the southern ones near rue Gay-Lussac. An aqueduct ran all the way from the Rungis basin near present-day Orly airport to supply them with water.

Cardo ran along present-day rue Saint-Jacques
Three bath complexes at Cluny, College de France, rue Gay-Lussac

script_body: In the 13th century, the Latin Quarter became the centre of learning for all of Western Europe. The first official reference to the Universitas Magistrorum et Scolarium Parisiensium dates from 1221. Initially it had no permanent home — teaching took place in the open air, on Place Maubert and mainly on rue de Fouarre nearby. Teachers stood on wooden trestles while students sat on their own fodder — 'fouarre' in old French — hence the street's name. Brawls and political agitation were so bad that in 1358 the Regent and future Charles V had the street barred with chains on both sides. Among the greatest thinkers who came to teach: Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, and Brunetto Latini, master of Dante. Dante himself came to study on rue de Fouarre in the early 14th century.
key_claims: University of Paris reference dates from 1221
Dante studied on rue de Fouarre
source_passage: The first official written reference to the Universitas Magistrorum et Scolarium Parisiensium dates from 1221

script_body: In 1253, a college was founded by Robert, the chaplain and confessor of Saint Louis. Born to a humble family in the village of Sorbon in the Ardennes, he became so great a scholar that the King had him dine at his table. The college became the seat of the faculty of theology and was known as La Sorbonne, after the native village of its founder. Its expansion was so spectacular that it soon overshadowed other institutions and many foreigners still mistake it for the entire University of Paris.
key_claims: Named after village of Sorbon in Ardennes
source_passage: One such college was founded in 1253 by Robert, the chaplain and confessor of Saint Louis

script_body: The enterprising Richelieu, who had been a student and later became dean of the Sorbonne, undertook its renovation. He laid the cornerstone of its chapel in 1635, designed by architect Jacques Lemercier. However, Richelieu's project was purely architectural — little was done to reform the curriculum, which until the Revolution remained restricted to theology. The beautiful compound, the work of Lemercier and Le Brun, was given rough treatment by the anti-clerical Revolutionaries. It was entirely reconstructed and expanded in the 19th century, including faculties of science and letters, inaugurated in 1901 with murals by Puvis de Chavannes.

script_body: In May 1968, a wind of revolt blew across the planet. Students transformed the Latin Quarter into a battlefield — not from premeditated political motivation but from a vague discontent with capitalism, imperialism, consumerism, and bourgeois rigidity. 'L'imagination au pouvoir' was scribbled on many a wall. Barricades were erected on all main arteries, cobblestones were dug from ancient streets and hurled at riot police, trees along the boulevards were felled. By autumn, the riots had died out. But the State proceeded to dismantle and decentralize the University, scattering students across the Paris area into numbered compounds — Paris I through XIII. The Latin Quarter lost its old cobbled streets, replaced with dull asphalt, and the arrondissement was forever changed.
physical_cues: asphalted streets where cobblestones once were
key_claims: University decentralized into Paris I through XIII
source_passage: in 1968, a wind of revolt blew across the planet, from the Latin Quarter to Prague

script_body: Napoleon restructured French higher education by founding the celebrated Grandes Ecoles — elite engineering schools outside the university framework. The most prestigious, the Ecole Polytechnique, trains France's top mathematicians and remains a military school. Its cadets, the celebrated 'X', take part in the 14 July parade down the Champs-Elysees. Until 1976, it was located in the heart of the Latin Quarter in the premises of the medieval College de Navarre on rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Genevieve. Its transfer to Palaiseau deprived the Quarter of some festive pomp — previously, on ceremonial occasions, cadets could be seen passing in their Napoleonic uniforms bearing slender swords.
physical_cues: rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Genevieve (former Polytechnique site)
key_claims: Ecole Polytechnique most prestigious military school
Located at College de Navarre until 1976 transfer to Palaiseau
source_passage: The Ecole Polytechnique, the most prestigious of them all, trains France's top mathematicians

script_body: The medieval Latin Quarter was a world of scholarly mischief. Neighbourhood taverns and brothels supplied the rowdy student population with cheap wines fit to 'boil the potted heads of wolves.' This was the Quarter that Francois Villon roamed in the 15th century, and of which Rabelais gave a saucy account. Favourite pranks included placing fried turds in graduates' hoods, pinning fox-tails or hare's ears to students' buttocks, making dogs run about with pots tied to their tails, and harassing maidservants. The church was a special target among these roguish, anticlerical youths. In Rabelais' story, the hero Pantagruel comes to study in Paris and visits the world-renowned library of the Abbey of Saint-Victor, which on the eve of the Revolution contained nearly 40,000 volumes and over 20,000 manuscripts.
physical_cues: Latin Quarter streets around the Sorbonne
source_passage: This was the Latin Quarter that Francois Villon roamed a century later and of which Rabelais gave a saucy account

script_body: When the Hundred Years' War broke out, the University — which had gradually lost its earlier privileges — sided with the English against the King of France and, later, against Jeanne d'Arc. Paris was in ruins, the territory of wolves, and the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve had become an 'annexe of Oxford.' In due course peace was restored and in 1437 the University submitted to the secular authority of Charles VII.
key_claims: University sided with English during Hundred Years' War
source_passage: the University sided with the English against the King of France and, later, against Jeanne d'Arc

script_body: Place Maubert — 'la Maube' — had been home to rowdy students and ruffians since the Middle Ages, a place of crime, vice, and public executions. Erasmus called it 'the cesspit of la Maube.' In the early 20th century it was frequented by terrifying 'Apaches' and hoodlums. In Down and Out in Paris and London, published in 1933, George Orwell described the neighbouring rue du Pot-de-Fer — where he lived at number 6 — as 'a ravine of tall, leprous houses, lurching towards one another in queer attitudes, as though they had all been frozen in the act of collapse.' Amidst destitute Arabs, Poles, and Italians, respectable French shopkeepers quietly piled up small fortunes.

script_body: In 451, Attila the Hun was at the gates of Paris with his army. The terrified population was ready to flee the left bank, but Genevieve bolstered their courage, prophesying that Paris would be spared. Though romanticized as a shepherdess in the 17th century, Genevieve was born in Nanterre to a well-to-do Roman father and a Greek mother. She led an ascetic life devoted to the poor and sick, performed miracles, and her prophecy came true. She became the patron saint of Paris. It was under her guidance — and through the influence of his wife Clotilde — that King Clovis converted to Christianity and made Paris his capital. The basilica of Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul was built on this hilltop site, receiving in its crypt both Clovis, who died in 511, and Genevieve, who died in 512 aged 89.
key_claims: Clovis converted under Genevieve and Clotilde
source_passage: in 451 Attila the Hun was at the gates of Paris with his 700,000 men

script_body: Genevieve's reliquary, fashioned around 630 by the famous Saint Eloi — patron of goldsmiths and later minister to King Dagobert I — was chiselled in gold and studded with gems. In times of floods, epidemics, and calamities, following a day of penitence and fasting, it would be carried in procession to Notre-Dame through streets decked with multicoloured drapery and strewn with flowers, to the continuous chiming of all the city's church bells. The story goes that during a raging epidemic in 1130, all were cured except three sceptics who would not prostrate themselves and therefore died. By 1725 there had been 114 such processions. In November 1793, the Revolution stripped the reliquary of its precious stones and sent it to the Mint. Genevieve's remains were burnt on Place de Greve.
source_passage: Genevieve's reliquary was fashioned in 630 by the famous Saint Eloi

script_body: In November 1793, the Revolution's anti-clerical fervour reached Saint Genevieve. Her reliquary was stripped of its precious stones and sent to the Mint to be melted down. Against all logic, the remains of Saint Genevieve — who had embodied precisely the same ideals as the Revolution, feeding the poor and defending Paris — were burnt on Place de Greve. In one fell swoop, the Revolution destroyed twelve hundred years of devotion. The wooden sculptures of the reliquary survived, though they lost their arms, and are now in the Louvre. In 1803, a fragment of the saint's sarcophagus was discovered in the crypt and placed in a new reliquary above the altar of Saint-Etienne-du-Mont, where it remains today.
source_passage: In November 1793 the reliquary was stripped of its precious stones and sent to the Mint to be melted down

script_body: The Revolution swept away the great Abbey of Sainte-Genevieve, founded in the 7th century by monks who settled next to Genevieve's holy shrine. But vestiges survive, now part of the Lycee Henri IV: medieval vaults, kitchens, a refectory, a cloister, the grand staircase dating from the 18th century, and the dome of the abbey's magnificent library. The square church tower on rue Clovis is the only element remaining in its original position. The abbey was a great place of learning, closely bound with the medieval University — its abbot held the post of chancellor and presented diplomas to graduates.

medieval vaults visible through school gate
key_claims: Square tower on rue Clovis only element in situ
source_passage: Only the square church tower on rue Clovis remains in situ

script_body: The Italian campaigns of 1515 impressed upon Francois I the artistic and intellectual achievements of Italy compared to the fossilized University of Paris. In 1530, to counteract its dogmatic theology and propagate the humanistic ideal of the Renaissance, he founded the College de France next to the Sorbonne. First known as Le College des Trois Langues — Hebrew and Greek were taught alongside Latin — it was soon renamed the College du Roi. Lectures were given in French, a revolution in itself. Over the centuries, the number of chairs grew from the initial three to over 40, but its principles have never changed: it remains independent of the University and its lectures are still free and open to the public. Among its illustrious professors were the historian Michelet, Champollion who deciphered the Egyptian hieroglyphs, the physicist Ampere, and the philosopher Bergson.
