script_body: At number 56 rue Jacob stood the Hotel d'York, where on 3 September 1783 at 9 am, the peace treaty between England and the United States of America was signed by the English representative David Hartley and his American counterparts Benjamin Franklin, John Jay and John Adams. Adams returned with his family the following September while looking for a permanent home, eventually settling in Auteuil. Nearby at number 52, Benjamin Franklin had already stayed at the Hotel de Hambourg in 1777, while waiting for permanent lodging before moving to Passy.
key_claims: Signed by Hartley, Franklin, Jay, Adams
Franklin stayed at Hotel de Hambourg 1777
source_passage: N 56 at the time was the Hotel d'York, where the peace treaty between England and the United States of America was signed at 9 am, on 3 September 1783

script_body: Behind the fence at number 20 rue Jacob was the 'sanctuary' of Natalie Barney, the glamorous Amazon who rode in the Bois de Boulogne wearing a bowler hat and black bow tie. For 60 years, French and American literati gathered in this shady courtyard with its creeping ivy. A mock Greek temple, Le Temple de l'Amitie, provided hedonistic atmosphere and shelter from the cold. When Barney arrived in 1909, tea and cake were the rule, but when the expatriates turned up in the 1920s, she reluctantly switched to champagne and whisky. Paul Valery read his works here but dropped her once elected an Academicien. Georges Antheil rehearsed his scandalous Ballet mecanique in the temple.
physical_cues: courtyard visible through fence at n 20
key_claims: Natalie Barney lived here 60 years from 1909
source_passage: the 'sanctuary' of Natalie Barney, the glamorous Amazon

script_body: At number 44 rue Jacob, the Hotel d'Angleterre welcomed many literary visitors over the centuries. Sherwood Anderson recommended it to the newly-wed Hemingways when they arrived in Paris in December 1921. Anderson himself had reportedly paid 75 cents per night for a double room. The lovely 18th-century building now has a patio for breakfast on fine days.
source_passage: Sherwood Anderson paid 75 cents per night for a double room, and therefore recommended it to the newly-wed Hemingways

script_body: On 2 September 1792, this bustling junction served as a recruiting ground for volunteers for 'the defence of the motherland' — in reality, for the three-day slaughter of the September Massacres. The first four victims, new detainees on their way to the abbey prison, were slain at this very street junction by the delirious mob. In 1848, a barricade was erected here on the first day of that year's Revolution, to the fervent cries of 'Vive la Republique!' Today this is a place of peace and fun, especially when the jazz musicians are about.
physical_cues: junction of rue de Buci and rue de Seine
source_passage: On 2 September 1792 it was a fine recruiting-ground for volunteers for the defence of the motherland

script_body: The Tour de Nesle earned an even darker reputation in medieval legend. According to the poet François Villon, one queen of France would lure passers-by up to the tower at night. After exhausting them, she would have them tied in sacks and dropped into the Seine below. Whether Marguerite, Jeanne, or Blanche inspired the tale — or none of them — the story became one of the most enduring legends of medieval Paris.
physical_cues: plan on eastern wing facade showing original Tour de Nesle location
Seine flowing below the Institut de France
key_claims: Villon Ballade des dames du temps jadis references the tower
Legend of queen luring passers-by and drowning them in sacks
source_passage: According to the poet Francois Villon, one queen would lure passers-by to the tower

script_body: The French like things big — and in the 17th century, Saint-Sulpice's parish was swollen with pride. The northern tower rises 73 metres, four metres taller than Notre-Dame, making it the highest point on the entire Left Bank. But this colossus was built in stages by six successive architects over more than a century, the last being the famous Chalgrin. Anne of Austria laid the cornerstone in 1646; the ubiquitous Louis Le Vau was brought in to redesign and enlarge the church, but died before seeing it through. Crucially, the southern tower was never actually completed — leaving the asymmetry that still jars the eye today. Henry Miller had his own critique: he called them 'fat belfries.'
key_claims: Six successive architects; Chalgrin the last
source_passage: the northern tower rising 73 metres above the ground, 4 metres more than Notre-Dame

script_body: One of Saint-Sulpice's most notorious parishioners was baptized here: Talleyrand, born in 1754 at 4 rue Garancière just behind the church. He was later sent to study in the seminary that once stood opposite — but young Talleyrand had other priorities. He was repeatedly expelled for going over the wall for amorous rendezvous. The seminary's neighbour on rue Férou may have been part of the attraction: a celebrated actress of the Comédie-Française, Mademoiselle Luzy, lived there between 1770 and 1785.
key_claims: Talleyrand born 1754 at 4 rue Garancière, baptized Saint-Sulpice
Expelled from seminary for amorous rendezvous
source_passage: One of the church's parishioners was Talleyrand, born in 1854 at 4 rue Garanciére

script_body: The most famous works of art in Saint-Sulpice are Eugène Delacroix's mural paintings in the Chapelle des Saints-Anges — the first chapel on your right as you enter. Three works fill the space: Heliodorus Driven from the Temple, Jacob Wrestling with the Angel, and Saint Michael Slaying the Dragon in the dome above. Delacroix dedicated the last five years of his life to these paintings, working from 1856 to 1861 even as his health declined. The chapel was inaugurated in August 1861, just two years before his death.
physical_cues: Jacob Wrestling mural on left wall
key_claims: Three Delacroix murals: Heliodorus, Jacob, Saint Michael
source_passage: Delacroix's mural paintings in the Chapelle des Deux-Anges

script_body: Just inside the door of Saint-Sulpice stand two enormous shells mounted on marble pedestals — not ordinary holy water fonts. These were gifts from the Republic of Venice to François I, and Pigalle carved them into the form of seaweed with tentacles. The same Pigalle left a marble Virgin and Child at the far end of the church — a replacement for an earlier statue that had been sent to the Mint during the Revolution. That lost statue had reportedly been cast from silver cutlery that the artist Languet de Cergy systematically pilfered from dinner parties. It had been nicknamed Notre-Dame de la Vaisselle: Our Lady of the Crockery.
physical_cues: Two giant shell holy water stoups
Pigalle's marble Virgin and Child in Chapelle de la Vierge
key_claims: Conch shells given to François I by Venice
Earlier Virgin nicknamed Notre-Dame de la Vaisselle
source_passage: two great conches mounted on a marble socle, which were offered to Francois I by the Republic of Venice

script_body: Look down at the floor of Saint-Sulpice and you'll see a copper strip running from the south transept to an obelisk in the north transept. This is a gnomon — an astronomical instrument built to determine the spring equinox and thus calculate the exact date of Easter each year. A hole in the south transept window lets in a precise ray of sunlight at midday; on the relevant day, that ray travels along the copper strip and strikes a marked point on the obelisk. The method was devised by the watchmaker Henri Sully in 1727. Dan Brown later fictionalised this copper line as the 'Rose Line' in The Da Vinci Code — a claim the church famously refuted with a plaque inside the building.
key_claims: Gnomon to determine spring equinox / date of Easter
source_passage: This method of calculation was worked out by the watchmaker Henri Sully in 1727

script_body: Look up at the west end of Saint-Sulpice and you'll see the organ — originally designed by Chalgrin and reconstructed by Aristide Cavaillé-Coll in 1862. It was inaugurated on Easter Sunday, April 20, 1862. With over 7,000 pipes across five manuals, it remains Cavaillé-Coll's acknowledged masterpiece and one of the finest organs in the world. The church has been blessed with a distinguished succession of organists, including Marcel Dupré and Charles-Marie Widor, who famously wrote his Toccata — perhaps the most recognised organ piece in the world — for this very instrument.
physical_cues: Organ case at west end of nave
key_claims: Widor wrote Toccata for this instrument
source_passage: originally designed by Chalgrin and reconstructed by Cavaillé-Coll in 1862. With its 6,500 pipes

script_body: Rue Servandoni is named for the Italian architect who designed Saint-Sulpice's imposing facade — and the street still holds a remarkable secret at number 15. A plaque marks the spot where the philosopher Condorcet, a Girondin denounced for refusing to vote for the death sentence on Louis XVI, took shelter in July 1793, offered refuge by the widow of sculptor François Vernet. Blind to the Terror around him, he spent eight months writing his Esquisse des progrès de l'esprit humain — a treatise on human progress — while a revolution tried to kill him. He finally left in disguise on 25 March 1794, was caught almost immediately, sent to prison, and committed suicide on 6 April.
source_passage: Condorcet, denounced for not having voted for the death sentence on Louis XVI

script_body: The neighbourhood around Saint-Sulpice remains the stronghold of Catholicism in Paris — but the seminary that once defined it is long gone. After the Revolution swept away the original two seminaries, a new one was built in 1820 on the southern side of the square. In 1906, following the vote for separation of church and state, the government took over the seminary and handed it to the Ministry of Finance. What remained was a tree-shaded alley along rue Bonaparte, l'Allée du Séminaire, and a neighbourhood full of shops selling religious items, ceremonial gowns, and theological books.
physical_cues: Religious goods shops on Place Saint-Sulpice
Rue Férou wall of old seminary
key_claims: After 1906 given to Ministry of Finance
source_passage: In 1906, after the vote for the separation of state and church, the government took over the seminary

script_body: Before this tidy covered market stood here, the Foire Saint-Germain was the wildest party in Paris — a place where acrobats, tightrope dancers, and animal tamers entertained every social class, including the King himself. Henri III mingled with jeering crowds, and the poet Scarron chronicled the debauchery, prostitution, and murders that flourished where wine flowed freely. Then, on the night of 16–17 March 1762, a gigantic fire consumed the entire fair in five hours. The flames even reached Saint-Sulpice, damaging the Chapel of the Virgin. The new fair that rose in its place never recaptured the magic. Closed during the Revolution, replaced by a market in the early 19th century, stripped of two-thirds of its area in 1898, it nearly disappeared entirely. Today the soul is gone — but stand here a moment and imagine the acrobats.
physical_cues: Covered market building at rue Mabillon and rue Clément
Old houses at 6, 8, 10 rue de Mabillon
key_claims: Fire 16–17 March 1762 consumed the fair in five hours
Flames reached Saint-Sulpice's Chapel of the Virgin
In 1898 lost two thirds of its area
source_passage: It took only five hours for the fair to be consumed by a gigantic fire on the night of 16 - 17 March 1762.

script_body: The street you just walked down — rue Clément — once passed through a gate called La Porte de Treille, the main entrance to one of Paris's great medieval fairs. And rue Mabillon? It was simply known as rue de la Foire: Street of the Fair. The Foire Saint-Germain was a city within a city, with over a hundred trading stalls. The restaurant at number 10 rue de Mabillon still commemorates the Compagnons Charpentiers du Devoir de Liberté — the carpenters' guild — through its decoration and an adjoining museum. Look up at the old houses at 6, 8, and 10: they are the last witnesses of a world that burned to ashes in 1762.
physical_cues: Old houses at 6,8,10 rue de Mabillon
key_claims: Rue Clément led to fair through La Porte de Treille
Rue Mabillon was known as rue de la Foire
Restaurant at no. 10 commemorates Compagnons Charpentiers
source_passage: Rue Clément led to the fair through a gate known as La Porte de Treille and rue Mabillon was known simply as rue de la Foire
entities: Compagnons Charpentiers du Devoir de Liberté

script_body: The poet Paul Scarron was a regular at the Foire Saint-Germain, famously arriving in his 'notorious invalid's chair' — he suffered from a severe rheumatic disorder that paralyzed him from his late twenties. He captured the fair's dark energy in verse: 'Fair, the element of gallants / Of rogues and of robbers / Fair where fewer trinkets are sold / Than human flesh.' It's a razor-sharp portrait of a place that was Paris's greatest entertainment and its most dangerous corner.
key_claims: Scarron attended the fair in his invalid's chair
Scarron wrote a poem describing the fair
source_passage: The poet Scarron, who would come here in his notorious invalid's chair

script_body: This unpretentious café overlooking Visconti's fountain was a gathering place for literary Paris in the 1920s. Hemingway wrote about the pigeons perched on the statues of the four bishops here; Henry Miller mentioned them in Tropic of Cancer. Faulkner, Fitzgerald, and Beckett were regulars. But the most charged moment happened in 1951: the last meeting between Jean-Paul Sartre and Albert Camus took place at this very café. The two quarrelled and parted company — permanently. Two of the 20th century's greatest minds, ending a friendship at a table you could sit at today.
physical_cues: Visconti fountain with four bishop statues
key_claims: Hemingway described pigeons on fountain in A Moveable Feast
Henry Miller mentioned them in Tropic of Cancer
Last meeting between Sartre and Camus here in 1951
source_passage: The last meeting between Sartre and Camus took place here in 1951

script_body: After the assassination of Henri IV, his widow Marie de Medici felt estranged at the Louvre and homesick for Florence. She bought the Hôtel du Petit-Luxembourg in 1611 and commissioned Salomon de Brosse to build an Italian-style palace. De Brosse, inspired by native genius, built a French one instead — the Palais du Luxembourg stands between its courtyard and gardens in the French manner. To flatter her, Rubens painted 24 narrative paintings on her life for the west wing. The palace took 15 years to complete (1615–1630), but barely had she settled in than Richelieu — the friend she had promoted — outmanoeuvred her politically. She was banished, died in Cologne in total destitution, and the second set of Rubens paintings she had planned, about Henri IV, was never made.
physical_cues: Palace facade from rue de Vaugirard
source_passage: The palace took 15 years to complete (1615-1630)

script_body: During the Terror, the Palais du Luxembourg had a grim second act: it became a prison. Eight hundred prisoners were kept here, a third of whom were guillotined — among them Danton and Camille Desmoulins. When the storm subsided the building was wrecked. Repairs began in 1804 under Chalgrin, who transferred the main staircase to the west wing and created a new auditorium. The palace then served as a seat for the Directoire, then the Senate, then the Chamber of Peers during the Restoration.
key_claims: One-third guillotined including Danton and Desmoulins
source_passage: 800 prisoners were kept here, a third of whom were guillotined, among them Danton and Camille Desmoulin

script_body: Marie de Medici devoted most of her attention to the garden. She had 2,000 elms planted and — emulating the Romans of ancient Lutetia — commissioned an aqueduct built all the way from Arcueil, in the southern suburbs, to supply the fountains of her new Eden. The aqueduct took Salomon de Brosse 11 years to complete. Today the aqueduct is gone but the garden's spirit remains: the Order of the Chartreux once occupied the land to the south, growing succulent fruit. Their tradition lives on in the fruit orchards on the southern edge of the gardens, where two tons of fruit are produced yearly — including raspberries, blackcurrants, figs, and over 200 varieties of pears and apples.
key_claims: 2,000 elms planted by Marie de Medici
Aqueduct from Arcueil by Salomon de Brosse over 11 years
Two tons of fruit yearly incl. 200 varieties pears/apples
source_passage: she had an aqueduct built all the way from Arcueil

script_body: Before the Luxembourg Gardens existed, this land was dominated by a sinister medieval castle: the Château de Vauvert. Its origins are lost, but it may have been the home of King Robert II the Pious in the late 10th century, banished from his palace on the Île de la Cité after the Pope forced him to renounce his beloved wife. For generations the castle was said to be haunted by the Devil, and no-one dared walk past it. The French expression aller au diable Vauvert — to go somewhere dangerously far away — still in use today, comes from that deeply-rooted fear. The Chartreux monks arrived in a beautiful procession on 21 November 1257, accepted the grounds from Saint Louis, and apparently frightened the Devil away for good.
physical_cues: Southern end of gardens near Boulevard Saint-Michel
No. 64 Boulevard Saint-Michel — former Chartreux entrance
key_claims: Château de Vauvert possibly home of Robert II the Pious
Expression 'aller au diable Vauvert' from the haunted castle
source_passage: The expression aller au diable Vauvert (to go on a dangerous journey), still in use, refers to that deeply-rooted fear

script_body: The Luxembourg Gardens we see today are a shadow of what they once were. After the Chartreux were expelled following the Revolution, the gardens briefly extended all the way to Boulevard du Montparnasse — colossal by Parisian standards. Then the real-estate market took over: chunks were cut off to widen rue de Vaugirard, open Boulevard Saint-Michel, and make way for rue de Médicis. The public was outraged. The imperial couple was booed at the Odéon. Petitions poured in — one bearing 12,000 signatures. None of it worked. The customary minimal concession was made: Chalgrin's Avenue de l'Observatoire was allowed to survive. The present gardens date from the Second Empire.
physical_cues: Garden boundaries hemmed in by rue de Vaugirard
key_claims: Once extended to Boulevard du Montparnasse
Present gardens date from Second Empire
source_passage: one of them bore 12,000 signatures

script_body: At the heart of the Luxembourg Gardens stands the famous central octagonal basin, encircled by 50 sculpted female heroines of the history of France. For generations, Latin Quarter students have deserted their austere libraries to bask in the sun on chairs ranked neatly around the water. Little children come to float model boats on the shimmering surface. Writers and poets have come here to think, to argue, and to recover from the intensity of the Left Bank's intellectual life. The basin is not just a fountain — it's the social centre of the gardens, the place where Hemingway first encountered Gertrude Stein as recalled in A Moveable Feast.
key_claims: Central basin encircled by 50 female heroines
Hemingway and Stein connection via A Moveable Feast
source_passage: the famous central octogonal basin, the hub of the gardens, encircled by 50 sculpted female heroines

script_body: Look for the small surprise tucked in the south section of the Luxembourg Gardens: a small-scale replica of the Statue of Liberty. It was planted here — alongside a tree of liberty — by the American Ambassador to Paris in June 1993, to commemorate the 200th anniversary of Franco-American friendship. It's an easy detail to walk past, but the gesture is real: these gardens, shaped in part by an Italian queen who dreamed of Florence, now hold a fragment of New York's most recognizable skyline.
physical_cues: Small Statue of Liberty replica in southwestern section
key_claims: Replica planted by US Ambassador June 1993
source_passage: planted by the American Ambassador to Paris in June 1993 to commemorate the 200th anniversary of Franco-American friendship

script_body: Before the Louvre opened to the public, France had another museum — this one. In 1750, the east wing of the Luxembourg Palace was opened to the public, the first time such a step had been taken in France. About 50 paintings from the King's collection were shown twice a week, and on those occasions visitors were also admitted to the west wing to see Rubens's 24 paintings on the life of Marie de Medici — now in the Louvre. The present museum, a different institution, opened only in 1865 in the orangery that Alphonse de Gisors had built 30 years earlier. Here were exhibited the works of the academic Pompiers, considered modern art by the bourgeoisie of the time.
key_claims: 1750 east wing opened to public — first in France
Present museum opened 1865 in orangery by Gisors
source_passage: In 1750 the east wing was opened to the public, the first time such a step was taken in France

script_body: Number 27 rue de Fleurus was the most important address in American literary Paris. Gertrude Stein lived here from 1903 to 1938, and her studio became a mecca for anyone who was anybody in the art world — provided they had a recommendation, unless she picked them up herself at Sylvia Beach's Shakespeare and Company. James Joyce was persona non grata. She called him 'a fifth-rate political schemer' and considered herself the main writer of the English language of the day. She dismissed Hemingway and his whole generation as 'a lost generation' — a phrase she borrowed from a garage owner who had used it about a young employee who'd been to war. The walls were hung with Renoir, Cézanne, Picasso, Braque, Matisse. It was Hemingway's idea of paradise.
source_passage: N° 27 on your left was the home of Gertrude Stein between 1903 and 1937

script_body: Rue Férou, behind Saint-Sulpice, has housed two of the 20th century's most iconic artists. In 1926, Hemingway moved here with Pauline Pfeiffer after leaving his wife Hadley — Pauline's Uncle Gus paid for the apartment at number 6. Here Hemingway worked on A Farewell to Arms. In 1951, Man Ray returned to Paris after the War and settled at 2 bis, into what his wife Juliet described as a space that 'looked like a garage.' Man Ray saw it differently: a whitewashed studio, flooded with light from skylights, open on three sides. He stayed until his death in 1976. Two artists, one quiet street, and a very different Paris separated by 25 years.
key_claims: Hemingway lived rue Férou from 1926 with Pauline Pfeiffer
Man Ray settled 2 bis in 1951, died 1976
source_passage: Man Ray settled in a sculptor's studio at n° 2 bis

script_body: Tucked away amidst dark vegetation in the Luxembourg Gardens, the Fontaine Médicis is the most romantically shaded corner of the park. The main grotto features the myth of Acis and Galatea surprised by the Cyclops Polyphemus. On the back face, added in 1866, is the Fontaine de Léda: Leda with Jupiter metamorphosed into a swan. The fountain was built around 1630 for Marie de Medici by architect Salomon de Brosse and rebuilt 1864–1866 by Alphonse de Gisors with sculpture by Auguste Ottin. It's a bliss during a heatwave, green and cool and forgotten by the crowds at the central basin.
physical_cues: Long narrow reflecting pool leading to grotto
Bronze figures of Acis and Galatea under arch
key_claims: Built c. 1630 by Salomon de Brosse for Marie de Medici
Rebuilt 1864–1866 by Gisors; sculpture by Auguste Ottin
source_passage: designed by the great Renaissance sculptor Jean Goujon

corrections.corrected: built c.1630 by Salomon de Brosse; rebuilt 1864–66 by de Gisors, sculptures by Ottin

script_body: In 1905 this modest guinguette with its plane-tree shade became ground zero for a revolution in art. Poets André Salmon and Paul Fort launched their magazine Vers et Prose here, sending out invitations — Salmon claimed 23,000 letters, Fort a more modest 10,000 — to every artist they could think of. The gambit worked: Montparnasse became the world capital of art, and La Closerie its beating heart. By 1912 Fort had been elected 'Prince des Poètes,' and every Tuesday night he presided over up to 200 writers, painters, musicians and critics. Picasso, Apollinaire, Max Jacob, Léon-Paul Fargue and Alfred Jarry were regulars. Jarry once drew a pistol, fired at the mirror, and told the horrified young woman beside him: 'Now that the ice is broken, let us talk!'
physical_cues: Terrace on the corner of Boulevard du Montparnasse and Avenue de l'Observatoire
key_claims: Vers et Prose launched 1905 by Salmon and Fort
Paul Fort elected Prince des Poètes 1912
Tuesday-night gatherings of up to 200 artists
source_passage: In 1905 La Closerie des Lilas was put on the map

script_body: La Closerie des Lilas has never had a single lilac. Not one. When it first opened in the 1840s as a simple outdoor tavern — a guinguette — it sat under plane trees, not lilacs. The lilacs belonged to a rival establishment across the Boulevard, and the name was simply borrowed. The café stood at the edge of the Latin Quarter, a convenient stop for stage-coaches heading to Fontainebleau, and it was already pulling in Baudelaire, Verlaine, Strindberg and Oscar Wilde before anyone had heard of Montparnasse.
physical_cues: Corner of Boulevard du Montparnasse and Avenue de l'Observatoire
key_claims: No lilacs ever grew at La Closerie; name borrowed
Originally a guinguette, a stop for Fontainebleau stage-coaches
Baudelaire, Verlaine, Strindberg and Wilde frequented it
source_passage: Despite its name, La Closerie has never had lilacs

script_body: When Hemingway returned from Canada with his newborn son Bumby in early 1924, he found La Closerie quiet and melancholy — a portrait immortalised by Paul Fort as 'Café des ombres.' For Hemingway, who lived just a few doors down at 113 rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs above a noisy sawmill, this was perfect. He came here to escape the racket and write. It was here that he worked on The Sun Also Rises, met Scott Fitzgerald and read the manuscript of The Great Gatsby, and read parts of The Torrents of Spring to John Dos Passos.
physical_cues: View up Avenue de l'Observatoire toward Ney's statue
key_claims: Hemingway returned from Canada with Bumby in early 1924
Wrote The Sun Also Rises at La Closerie
Met Fitzgerald; read Great Gatsby manuscript
Read Torrents of Spring to Dos Passos
source_passage: When Hemingway, back from Canada with the newborn Bumby, discovered the Closerie in 1924

script_body: This bronze hero with sword aloft was one of Napoleon's greatest marshals — 'le Brave des braves' — and it cost him his life. After Napoleon's Hundred Days return, the Restoration government could not forgive Ney for rejoining his emperor. The Tribunal of Peers, meeting at the Palais du Luxembourg, condemned him for high treason despite a brilliant defence. On 7 December 1815 he was led to the corner of Avenue de l'Observatoire and Boulevard du Port-Royal and shot by a firing squad. The statue by sculptor François Rude was unveiled on the 38th anniversary of that execution — 7 December 1853 — erected on the very spot. When the Port-Royal railway station was extended, it was moved to its present location, where Hemingway liked to stop and contemplate 'my old friend, the statue of Marshal Ney with his sword out.'
physical_cues: Bronze statue of Ney with sword raised
key_claims: Condemned by Tribunal of Peers at Palais du Luxembourg
source_passage: On 7 December 1815, Ney was led to the present corner of Avenue de l'Observatoire and Boulevard du Port-Royal and shot

script_body: Step along Avenue de l'Observatoire and you come face to face with one of Paris's most spectacular pieces of public sculpture. Jean-Baptiste Carpeaux's fountain, completed in 1874, shows four women — representing Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas — their bodies twisting dynamically as they support a great celestial sphere, the zodiac band encircling it. Horses rear in the basin below, and the whole composition conveys breathtaking movement. It sits on the axis of the Paris meridian, in the garden named for the explorer Marco Polo.
physical_cues: Four female bronze figures supporting the globe
source_passage: Carpeaux's impressive fountain, The Four Corners of the World

script_body: Before it was an address for artists and intellectuals, rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs was a country lane used to haul quarry stones. At the time of Catherine de Medici it was the route for transporting building material from the quarries south of Paris to her new Tuileries Palace under construction. By the late 19th century the lane had become a respectable address dotted with convents, attracting artists and professors who found its tranquillity appealing, though Balzac had earlier warned that 'robbery was the least of dangers one encountered there.'
physical_cues: Street running south from Boulevard du Montparnasse
Entrance to Ecole Alsacienne at no. 109
Gap in house numbers 111 to 115 bis

Balzac: 'robbery was the least of dangers'

script_body: The grand entrance at 109 rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs belongs to the Ecole Alsacienne, founded in 1874 by Protestant teachers and academics who had fled Alsace after the Franco-Prussian War. Their school became a testing ground for progressive education — humanities, openness, tolerance, but without sacrificing academic ambition. One of its earliest notable students was André Gide. The school was non-religious from the start and one of the first to go co-educational, making it a quiet act of resistance against the rigid Catholic hegemony that dominated French schooling.
key_claims: Founded 1874 by Protestant academics from Alsace
source_passage: the prestigious Ecole Alsacienne, which was founded in 1874

script_body: While the Ecole Alsacienne nurtured freethinkers, its neighbour Collège Stanislas represented the other end of the educational spectrum — traditional, Catholic, rigorous. A 1986 guidebook to the 6th arrondissement gave the Ecole Alsacienne a single line while being effusive about Stanislas, concluding: 'How many of its pupils have suffered its harsh discipline which shapes the best minds!' Among those minds was a young Charles de Gaulle, remembered by a fellow student who served at mass with the young Charles de Gaulle.
key_claims: Charles de Gaulle attended as a young boy; Roger Wild anecdote
source_passage: writer Roger Wild, who remembered having served at mass one day with a 14-year-old boy named Charles de Gaulle

script_body: Turn into rue Joseph-Bara and stop at number 3. This cluster of artists' studios — climbing erratically from street-level to the rooftop — was the social epicentre of Montparnasse in the 1920s. In 1913 the painter Kisling moved into the attic, romantically picturesque, baking in summer, freezing in winter. He didn't mind. His studio became the party hub for the entire Ecole de Paris: Modigliani, Cocteau, Radiguet, Max Jacob and Pascin all crowded in. Modigliani, put up by his art dealer Zborowski in the same building, only had to climb the stairs. André Salmon moved across the street when he married. The morning after one wild party Kisling was heard to complain: 'They have peed on my sketches!'
physical_cues: Irregular studio building with pitched grey roof
key_claims: Modigliani, Zborowski and Pascin in same building
Social hub of Montparnasse années folles
source_passage: His attic became the social hub of Montparnasse, especially during the crazy years

script_body: Tucked behind the respectable facade of rue d'Assas at number 100 bis is an oasis: the home and studio of sculptor Ossip Zadkine. He arrived in Paris with nothing, endured years of destitution, and never romanticised the experience. By 1928 he could afford to buy this provincial house with its enchanting garden, and he never left. Today it is a free city museum, richly endowed with some 400 sculptures, drawings and lithographs he bequeathed to Paris. The garden is still filled, as he described it, with the song of birds.
physical_cues: Garden with sculptures among trees and birdsong
key_claims: Zadkine settled at 100 bis rue d'Assas in 1928, died 1967
source_passage: Zadkine hated the life of destitution he was forced to live during his first years in Paris

script_body: At 6 rue de Chevreuse the exquisite premises of Reid Hall hide behind an unassuming street facade. Elisabeth Mills Reid, wife of Whitelaw Reid, the American minister to France, bought the property in 1893 and established the American Girls' Club — a hall of residence for young American women, mostly art students, who came to Paris seeking a creative education denied them at home. At the outbreak of World War One the building was converted into a military hospital. Today it is a Columbia University global centre, its beautiful garden still open to curious visitors.
key_claims: Founded as American women's residence by Mrs Reid
source_passage: at n° 6 are the superb premises of Reid Hall

script_body: Rue de la Grande-Chaumière became the indispensable art school of Montparnasse, offering the freedom of expression that the Beaux-Arts denied. The Académie at number 14 opened in 1902 and its sister academy Colarossi was next door at number 10. Every Monday morning a 'models' fair' was held on the corner with Boulevard du Montparnasse, where artists chose from Italian models. A three-hour session cost five francs — a luxury only established artists could afford. Under Bourdelle the Russian and Polish painters of the Ecole de Paris found guidance here; a generation later, Giacometti and Léger were among the teachers.
physical_cues: Académie de la Grande-Chaumière at no. 14
Art supply shops on the street
key_claims: Bourdelle taught sculpture here; later Giacometti and Léger
Monday models' fair on street corner
source_passage: specifically at the Académie de la Grande-Chaumiére at n° 14

script_body: At the junction of rue Vavin you'll spot a building that looks like it belongs on a Métro platform. The striking stepped-terrace apartment block at number 26, designed by Henri Sauvage and built in 1912–14, is entirely clad in white and blue glazed ceramic tiles — hence its nickname 'Carreaux Métro.' Each upper floor is set back from the one below, giving each apartment a terrace and flooding the building with light. Sauvage chose the tiles for hygiene as much as beauty — easy to wash, easy to maintain. It was a radical idea for its time, patented in 1912, and it still draws architectural pilgrims today.
physical_cues: White and blue ceramic tile facade
Contrast with Haussmann buildings either side
source_passage: the extraordinary building at n° 26, put up by the architect Sauvage in 1912

script_body: The Rotonde started life as a shoe shop. In 1911 Victor Libion bought it, knocked through to a café, and fell in love with his artist clientele. He subscribed to foreign newspapers on their behalf, looked the other way when a croissant disappeared, and let customers sit for hours over an empty cup. He collected their paintings for the walls and created the atmosphere that made Montparnasse. But when he extended that same generosity to Russian revolutionaries — Lenin and Trotsky among them — and refused to inform on them to police, he signed his own ruin. The police eventually closed him down over American cigarettes. Libion sold up, moved south, and died a broken man, having been cheated out of the very Modigliani paintings he'd been given in lieu of café bills.
physical_cues: Corner of Boulevard du Montparnasse and Boulevard Raspail
key_claims: Started as shoe shop, bought by Libion 1911
Libion subscribed to foreign newspapers for artists
Police closed him over American cigarettes
source_passage: The Rotonde started as a shoe shop, which was bought by Libion in 1911

script_body: By the early 1910s La Rotonde had become the unofficial embassy of the Ecole de Paris. Modigliani, Soutine, Picasso, Apollinaire, Rivera — they all passed through. Modigliani's passionate, short-lived affair with English poetess Beatrice Hastings played out across these café tables. It was the new centre of gravity for the colony of painters who had outgrown La Closerie — until the Rotonde too lost its soul when Libion sold up.
physical_cues: Historic photos of original café displayed inside
key_claims: New centre of gravity for Ecole de Paris from ~1912
source_passage: within a year the colony had migrated to a new centre of gravity at the newly-opened Carrefour Vavin

script_body: The Eiffel Tower was designed not by Eiffel himself but by two engineers in his company, Koechlin and Nouguier, whose project won the competition for a striking monument for the 1889 Universal Exhibition. The Exhibition officially commemorated the centenary of the French Revolution — among competing proposals was a gigantic guillotine in honour of the victims of the Terror. Rising approximately 312 metres, the Tower was twice the height of the tallest structure previously built by man. Despite its gigantic dimensions, the iron structure weighed roughly 7,300 tonnes — an awesome technical feat. Yet on 7 May 1889, the day of its solemn inauguration, none of the lifts worked.
physical_cues: Four great iron legs tapering to the summit
key_claims: Lifts didn't work on inauguration day
source_passage: Rising 318 metres above the ground, it was twice the height of the tallest construction hitherto ever built by man

script_body: Not everyone welcomed the Tower. A petition signed by fifty leading figures from arts and letters — including Guy de Maupassant, Charles Gounod, Alexandre Dumas, and Charles Garnier — condemned the 'monstrous construction' in the name of Art and Civilisation. They showered it with metaphors: 'hollow candlestick', 'solitary riddled suppository', 'bald umbrella', 'skeleton'. Maupassant, contemplating leaving Paris, settled instead for lunching in the second-floor restaurant — the only spot in the city from which the Tower could not be seen. The painter Robert Delaunay saw it differently, making the Tower his favourite subject.
key_claims: Petition of 50 artists/writers incl. Maupassant, Gounod, Dumas, Garnier
Maupassant dined in second-floor restaurant to avoid seeing it
Delaunay championed it in modern painting
source_passage: Guy de Maupassant, after an impulse to pack up and move out of the capital, decided instead to eat in the second-floor restaurant

script_body: The Tower was meant to be ephemeral — a temporary structure for the World's Fair — and in 1909 enemies intensified campaigns to demolish it, claiming it was useless. Its salvation came from its height: wireless telegraphy was emerging, and the tall iron tower made a marvellous antenna. The first spoken news bulletin was broadcast from the Eiffel Tower in 1925, and in 1935 France's first experimental television transmission was made from here — a milestone that a few dozen excited enthusiasts received on their sets.
key_claims: Temporary structure; saved by wireless use
source_passage: The first news bulletin was broadcast from the Eiffel Tower in 1925

script_body: On 31 March 1889, the second anniversary of the beginning of construction, a sixty-strong party of top-hatted and monocled dignitaries made the first official ascent. Prime Minister Gustave Tirard gave up at the first floor; most of the others followed. But Gustave Eiffel persevered, urging the last ten breathless participants to the summit, where — with Paris spread at his feet — the Minister of Trade awarded him the Légion d'honneur. The honour, the book notes, should rightly have been shared with the two original designers, Koechlin and Nouguier.
key_claims: Party of 60, PM Tirard gave up
Eiffel received Légion d'honneur at summit from Lockroy
source_passage: On 31 March 1889, the second anniversary of the beginning of its construction

script_body: The 1889 Universal Exhibition, and the Eiffel Tower at its heart, was not merely a celebration of engineering. The Third Republic, beleaguered by anarchists, revisionists and Boulangistes threatening its stability, organised the Exhibition to boost patriotic feeling and achieve political cohesion. It was to mark the Republic's recovery and trumpet France's entry into modernity — to dazzle the world and assert national prestige at a moment of profound internal vulnerability.
key_claims: Exhibition designed to boost patriotic cohesion
source_passage: the Third Republic, beleaguered by anarchists, revisionists and Boulangistes

script_body: Voltaire died at number 27 on 30 May 1778, aged 84. He had left the quai in 1723 finding it too noisy, but returned on 10 February 1778, and his host the Marquis de Villette gave him a room overlooking the quiet courtyard. When Voltaire's play Irène triumphed at the theatre, crowds pressed around his coach on the quai, then called quai des Théatins — named for the Order founded here by Mazarin in 1647. The Marquis illuminated the quai and replaced the street sign with a plaque reading quai Voltaire. Police removed it the next morning. The renaming only became official on 11 July 1791, when Voltaire's remains were transferred to the Panthéon.
key_claims: Voltaire died at no. 27 on 30 May 1778
Quai previously called quai des Théatins
source_passage: where Voltaire died on 30 May 1778, at the age of 84

script_body: The quai Voltaire reads like a roll-call of European culture. Delacroix lived at number 13 between 1829 and 1835, in a north-facing studio where the idea for his celebrated La Liberté Guidant le Peuple may have germinated. Corot came after; Ingres had a studio at number 17. Baudelaire lodged at number 19 between 1856 and 1858, working on Les Fleurs du Mal. Wagner completed Die Meistersinger here in the winter of 1861–62. Sibelius and Oscar Wilde also stayed at number 19. Alfred de Musset was at number 25 between 1839 and 1849.
physical_cues: Number 19 — hotel of Baudelaire, Wagner, Sibelius, Wilde
source_passage: Between 1829 and 1835 Delacroix lived on the 5th floor at n° 13

script_body: A mansion on the quai was occupied by Louise-Renée de Penacoët de Kéroualle, the artful mistress of Charles II of England, who used her charms to become Duchess of Portsmouth. Louis XIV valued her influence — it served his diplomatic dealings with England. When Charles II died, the Duchess removed as many works of art as she could carry from his magnificent collection and crammed them into her quai Voltaire residence.
physical_cues: Antique shops now occupying some of these buildings
key_claims: Louise-Renée de Kéroualle was mistress of Charles II
Louis XIV used her for diplomacy
Removed artworks from Charles II's collection
source_passage: Louise-Renée de Penacoét de Kéroualle, the artful mistress of Charles II

script_body: The Hôtel de Tessé at number 1 was built on the site of a mansion that burned down in 1760 — along with its owner. The 80-year-old Marquis de Bacqueville had gone to the Opera knowing a fire had broken out in his house. When he returned and found it in flames, he walked back inside to rescue papers and never came out again. The same eccentric had, eighteen years earlier, fitted himself with two pairs of wings, launched from his rooftop, and attempted to fly across the Seine. His brief flight ended on a wash-shed on the river, and he with a broken leg.
key_claims: Marquis de Bacqueville died in 1760 fire
Earlier attempted to fly across the Seine with wings, broke a leg
source_passage: the 80-year-old Marquis de Bacqueville

script_body: At number 29, the Hôtel de Mailly-Nesle was home to five sisters, grand-daughters of the Duc de Mazarin. One by one they became mistresses of Louis XV — all but the third, kept under tight guard by her husband. The last, the Duchesse de Châteauroux, received an annual pension of 80,000 pounds from the royal lover. The mob called her 'La P... du Roi.' She died suddenly in 1744, aged only 27, in a first-floor room that still exists. By the following year, the Marquise de Pompadour had captured the King's heart.
key_claims: Five Mazarin grand-daughters at no. 29; four became mistresses of Louis XV
source_passage: Five delectable sisters, the grand-daughters of the Duc de Mazarin

script_body: Bouchardon's giant fountain, known as La Fontaine des Quatre Saisons, occupies numbers 57–59 rue de Grenelle. The four seasons are represented by chubby cupids — in spring flowers, harvesting, grape-picking (a frightened rabbit making a dash to escape), and sheltering under a blanket. Voltaire was unimpressed. He found the street too narrow for such an overbearing monument, and nicknamed it 'La Trompeuse' — the deceiver — because it contained 'so much stone for so little water.' There was some wisdom in the complaint: the fountains of Paris were supplied with filthy Seine water and contributed to cholera epidemics. The fountain is also literally deceptive: it is only a thin facing on a wall, a consequence of the nuns of the Recollettes refusing to surrender more than a narrow strip of their estate.
physical_cues: Massive stone facade towering over narrow street
key_claims: Bouchardon's fountain at 57–59 rue de Grenelle
Paris fountains supplied with Seine water, linked to cholera
Thin wall-facing because of the Recollettes nuns
source_passage: Bouchardon's gigantic fountain known as La Fontaine des Quatre Saisons

script_body: The church of Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin began as a Dominican noviciate, with its entrance on the now-demolished section of rue Saint-Dominique. Anne de Rohan-Montbazon, Duchesse de Luynes, laid the cornerstone on 5 March 1682. The Revolution dissolved the noviciate, but in 1804, when Christianity was no longer anathema, an enormous congregation gathered at the church's steps where Pope Pius VII gave them his blessing. It then became the parish church of the returning aristocratic émigrés of the Faubourg, their favourite place of worship.
source_passage: Anne de Rohan-Montbazon, Duchesse de Luynes, was living at the Hétel de Luynes when she came over to lay the cornerstone

script_body: In 1852, Aristide Boucicaut, a shop assistant at Au Petit Saint-Thomas on rue du Bac, was offered a partnership in a small hosiery shop, Au Bon Marché, at the corner of rue du Bac and rue de Sèvres. By 1863 he was its sole owner. Floor space grew from 30 square metres to 26,000 within sixty years. The extended premises used an iron structure involving Gustave Eiffel's firm (the 1872 expansion), the symbol of modernity. The story of Bon Marché is the story of triumphant capitalism — and Emile Zola explored its every mechanism to write his novel Au Bonheur des Dames.
physical_cues: Grand iron-and-glass building at 24 rue de Sèvres
key_claims: Floor space 30 → 26,000 sq m in 60 years
Zola's Au Bonheur des Dames modeled on it
source_passage: new extended premises had an iron structure, the symbol of modernity, and were designed by Gustave Eiffel

script_body: Emile Zola called the great department stores of Paris 'gigantic modern bazaars' and saw in them the engine of consumer society — destroying helpless small tradesmen in the process. The Bon Marché became the subject of his novel Au Bonheur des Dames: a world of sham, where the irresistible weapon of advertising lured the female client in, and where she was inevitably trapped, dazzled by overflowing goods and ever-changing fashions. Zola's relentless sociological mission was the exploration of how the machinery of 19th-century capitalism actually worked.
physical_cues: Overwhelming accumulation of goods on every floor
key_claims: Zola called department stores 'gigantic modern bazaars'
Bon Marché model for Au Bonheur des Dames
Zola explored dehumanising mechanics of retail capitalism
source_passage: These gigantic 'modern bazaars', as Emile Zola called them

script_body: Down rue de Babylone at number 57 bis stands one of Paris's most extraordinary buildings: a pagoda-shaped structure built in 1895–96 by architect Alexandre Marcel — an authentic Frenchman despite the design — reportedly commissioned by a manager of the Bon Marché in an attempt to win back his unfaithful wife. Japonisme was the rage, which perhaps should have charmed Madame. The Chinese legation, who briefly rented the premises, moved out when they discovered murals inside celebrating Japan's victories over China. The building was converted into a cinema in 1931 and remains the only picture-house in the 7th arrondissement.
physical_cues: Pagoda roofline and Japanese architectural details
key_claims: Chinese legation left over pro-Japan murals
source_passage: a pagoda-shaped cinema, built in 1895/6

script_body: Behind the gates of 57 rue de Varenne stands Hôtel Matignon, the Prime Minister's residence and arguably the most sumptuous mansion in the Faubourg. In 1808, Talleyrand moved in and immediately put his legendary chef Carême to work — lavish dinner parties four times a week for 36 privileged guests. Carême was the most celebrated cook of his age, the inventor of the towering pièce montée; in this gilded dining room he was at his peak. Three years later Talleyrand sold the hôtel to the state, perhaps needing the cash to fund the next regime he planned to survive.
physical_cues: Imposing gateway at 57 rue de Varenne
Glimpse of courtyard through gates when open
source_passage: The Hétel Matignon, at n° 57 rue de Varenne, is the residence of the Prime Minister and perhaps the most sumptuous mansion in the Faubourg.

script_body: The story of Hôtel Matignon reads like a history of French political instability. After Talleyrand sold it, the mansion passed to Louis XVIII, then the Duke of Galliera, whose widow lent it to the Comte de Paris — the Orléans pretender to the throne. When the Comte hosted his daughter's engagement party here, the Third Republic panicked and passed a law expelling the House of Orléans from France. The law lasted until after the Great War. When war broke out in 1914, the Prince d'Orléans came back to serve his country — and was promptly imprisoned for his trouble.
physical_cues: Closed gates of Matignon hinting at inaccessible interior
Garden foliage visible above perimeter wall
source_passage: Louis XVIII swapped it for the Palais de l'Elysée... the Third Republic passed a law expelling the princes of the House of Orléans from France.

script_body: Hidden behind the Prime Minister's gates is one of the largest private gardens in Paris — and at its heart, a bejewelled 18th-century folly built as a music room and nicknamed Le Petit-Trianon. While Versailles has its famous Trianon, the Faubourg has this intimate echo: a gilded retreat where the sounds of the harpsichord once floated through jasmine-scented air, unreachable by the public and all the more tantalizing for it.
physical_cues: Garden canopy visible over walls on rue de Varenne
source_passage: Besides splendid interior decoration, the Hotel Matignon has an immense garden with a bejewelled 18th-century folly, built as a music room and called Le Petit-Trianon.

script_body: Before it was a museum, the Hôtel de Biron was Paris's most bohemian commune. When the religious congregation was dissolved in 1904, the empty rooms were let to artists at a modest rent. In moved Rainer Maria Rilke, Isadora Duncan, Rodin — and a nineteen-year-old Jean Cocteau. Cocteau described looking out from his meagrely furnished former solfeggio classroom into the unkempt garden where Rodin worked among wild briars and forget-me-not. At night, he could see a light burning in the window where Rilke was writing deep into the night — working on 'The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge.'
physical_cues: Overgrown garden areas near boundary walls
source_passage: Rainer Maria Rilke, Isadora Duncan, Rodin and Jean Cocteau became the privileged tenants of these enchanting surroundings. Cocteau was 19 when he arrived.

script_body: The story of the Musée Rodin begins with a wigmaker. Monsieur Peyrenc de Moras, from Languedoc, had made such a staggering fortune speculating in John Law's paper-money schemes that he commissioned a great architect — while his neighbor Charlotte Desmares, who'd bet on the same market, went bankrupt. Peyrenc's mansion was fit for royalty: Louise de Bourbon, daughter-in-law of Louis XIV and Madame de Montespan, bought it from the wigmaker's widow in 1732.
physical_cues: Grand 18th-century facade on rue de Varenne
source_passage: Originally the hdtel was built for Monsieur Peyrenc, a wigmaker from Languedoc.

corrections.corrected: Primary architect Jean Aubert; Jacques Gabriel also involved

script_body: After the last private owner, the Duchesse de Charost, sold the Hôtel de Biron to a religious congregation in 1820, it became a school. In 1904, when French law dispersed the congregation, the school went public and the vast space was suddenly available. Rather than sell, someone had the inspired idea of renting rooms to artists cheaply — and so one of Paris's grandest private mansions became an accidental artists' commune, populated by the century's most influential creative minds.
physical_cues: Scale of the building suggesting institutional use
source_passage: Its last owner, the Duchesse de Charost, sold it to a religious congregation in 1820.

script_body: Paris loves novelty — and converting a railway station into a museum was bound to create a sensation. The Gare d'Orsay opened on the symbolic date of 14 July 1900, so beautiful that the painter Édouard Detaille suggested even then that it should become a museum. At its heart, the enormous Belle Époque dining room — with extravagant candelabras and an allegorical mural — has been preserved on the first floor, complete, while the magnificent vaulted glass-and-iron ceiling and the great station clock still preside over the converted nave below.
physical_cues: Giant station clock visible from the main hall
Belle Époque dining room on first floor
source_passage: this one was not inaugurated until 1900, on the symbolic date of 14 July, and was so beautiful that the painter Edouard Detaille suggested even then that it should be turned into a museum.

corrections.corrected: Inaugurated 1 December 1986, opened to public 9 December 1986

script_body: Although the Musée d'Orsay is devoted to all art forms developed in France in the second half of the 19th century — and hosts chamber-music concerts too — most visitors come for the Impressionist collection on the upper floors. Its fame is built on those galleries, though the building itself is equally extraordinary: a temple to modernity from the age of steam, echoing Monet's paintings of the Gare Saint-Lazare and Zola's novel 'La Bête humaine.'
physical_cues: Impressionist paintings on upper level galleries
Rooftop terrace with views across the Seine
source_passage: Although the museum is devoted to all the forms of art that developed in France in the second half of the 19th century, and hosts other activities such as chamber-music concerts, most visitors come for the Impressionist collection.

script_body: Here is a piece of Parisian irony: the Musée d'Orsay's destiny as a museum was proposed the very year it opened as a train station. In 1900, the painter Édouard Detaille — seeing the grand Beaux-Arts architecture — suggested on the spot that it should be turned into a museum or art gallery. It took another 86 years for someone to act on the idea. The Cour des Comptes next door, meanwhile, was utterly destroyed and replaced by the station; the Commune left few architectural survivors in this quarter.
physical_cues: Exterior Beaux-Arts facade on quai Anatole-France
Giant ornamental clock on Seine-facing facade
source_passage: The Cour des Comptes (the revenue court), on the other hand, was utterly destroyed and replaced by the Orsay railway station.

script_body: Around the corner from the museum, at 31 rue de Bellechasse, Alphonse Daudet lived from 1885 to 1897. Proust visited his widow here and wrote that he knew of no place 'so filled with the past, with thought, so piously consecrated by memory.' The building's dead include the mathematician Monge, the physician Villemin, and the historian Bainville. Around the corner at number 27, Gustave Doré had his studio — the building still bears his initials GD.
physical_cues: Initials GD carved or mounted at 27 rue de Bellechasse
source_passage: n° 31 on your right, where Alphonse Daudet lived between 1885 and 1897.

script_body: The elegant Hôtel de Salm across from the Musée d'Orsay has a tragic founding story. Its first owner, Prince Frédéric III of Salm-Kyrburg, sincerely supported the Revolution — yet was accused of being merely 'the mask of patriotism' and sent to the guillotine. He was so deeply in debt that by the time the mansion was completed, he no longer owned it; he had become a tenant in his own home. After his execution, his sister bought a plot in what is now the 12th arrondissement — the cemetery of Picpus — where his remains rest alongside those of 1,300 other victims of the Revolution.
physical_cues: Neoclassical facade facing the Seine and Musée d'Orsay
source_passage: The mansion was named after its first owner, Frédéric Ill, the Prince of Salm-Kyrburg, who, despite his sincere support of the Revolution, was accused of being 'but the mask of patriotism' and was sent to the guillotine.

corrections.original: six days before the fall of Robespierre
corrections.corrected: the day before the fall of Robespierre

script_body: After the Prince of Salm's execution, a former wigmaker named Claude Lenthereau had the audacity to reinvent himself as the 'Marquis de Beauregard.' He acquired the Hôtel de Salm, bought the jewel-like Château de Bagatelle on credit, kept a celebrated actress on a 10,000-pound pension, and threw unbelievably lavish banquets — all while Paris sneered. The satirical press dubbed him 'the foolishness of a parvenu rascal who, in order to efface any vestige of original powder, called himself the Marquis de Beauregard.' He was eventually unmasked, condemned, branded and put in irons for four years.
physical_cues: Restored neoclassical facade bearing no trace of the Commune fire
source_passage: Claude Lenthereau, a wigmaker who by the end of the Revolution called himself Marquis de Beauregard, became the next landlord of the Hotel de Salm.

script_body: Thomas Jefferson arrived in Paris in 1784 and, from his neighbor Lafayette's house at 123 rue de Lille, could admire the Hôtel de Salm under construction across the way. He brought other Americans to see it — the architect Charles Bulfinch and the painter John Trumbull — but most significantly Pierre L'Enfant, who is known to have been deeply inspired by Parisian architecture in designing the city of Washington D.C.
physical_cues: View of facade from quai Anatole-France
Alignment with Musée d'Orsay across the street
source_passage: Thomas Jefferson, who arrived in Paris in 1784, was a frequent guest at Lafayette's home at n° 123 rue de Lille.

script_body: The National Assembly's neoclassical facade is, technically, a lie — or at least a theatrical addition. Napoleon ordered it added in 1806 to the existing 18th-century Palais Bourbon so that it would mirror the Temple de la Gloire (today's Madeleine) across the Seine and across the Place de la Concorde. The symmetry is deliberate: a grand urban axis expressing French order. The Regency palace behind the facade was originally built for Louise-Françoise de Bourbon, legitimized daughter of Louis XIV and Madame de Montespan, by architects including Gabriel, Giardini, Lassurance and Aubert.
physical_cues: Neoclassical colonnade visible from Pont de la Concorde
Symmetry with La Madeleine on the opposite bank
source_passage: The Neo-classical fagade of the building, however, is only a facing: the Emperor, a fervent admirer of Classical art, added it in 1806 to the 18th-century Palais-Bourbon to match the front of the Madeleine.

script_body: Next door to the Palais Bourbon, the Hôtel de Lassay — now the home of the President of the National Assembly — is a masterpiece of Regency architecture. It is essentially a single elongated raised floor with a row of elegant French doors, surmounted by a sculpted balustrade carrying urns and clusters of chubby cupids. Inside, five spacious halls still used for official receptions were decorated with mirrors, carved doors and delicate paintings — the aesthetic of discreet architecture contrasted with sumptuous interior decoration, ideally suited to the pleasure-seeking inmates of the 18th century.
physical_cues: Balustrade with urns and cupids visible from the street
source_passage: The Hotel de Lassay consists essentially of a single, elongated, raised floor, with a row of elegant French doors along its front, surmounted by a sculpted balustrade carrying urns and clusters of chubby cupids - a masterpiece of Regency architecture.

script_body: On the streets running toward the Palais Bourbon, the Faubourg's grandeur has a darker underside. At 116 rue de Grenelle — now the Mairie of the 7th — the owner during Louis XVI's reign was the Duc de Brissac, Governor of Paris. On 9 September 1792, he was slain in the streets of Versailles during the September Massacres. His head was then sliced off and carried by the patriots all the way to Louveciennes — to be displayed before his ex-mistress, the Comtesse du Barry. She took the head back to Paris and buried it in the gardens, where it was discovered accidentally in 1901.
physical_cues: Mairie du 7e at 116 rue de Grenelle
source_passage: On 9 September 1792 the Duke was slain on the streets of Versailles, after which his head was sliced off and carried by the patriotes all the way to Louveciennes.

script_body: At the corner of rue de Bourgogne and rue de Grenelle — on the site of today's number 115 — lies the secret grave of Adrienne Lecouvreur, the most adulated actress of the Comédie-Française. When she died in 1730, the Church refused her Christian burial. The priest of Saint-Sulpice turned her away despite Voltaire's furious protest: she was carried by night to the river by three charitable souls, and buried here without ceremony. An 86-year-old admirer fixed a commemorative plaque under the portal of the Hôtel de Saumery built on the site in 1786. Her remains were searched for in 1797 at the instigation of the Comédie-Française — and never found.
physical_cues: Corner of rue de Bourgogne and rue de Grenelle at n°115
source_passage: On the corner of rue de Bourgogne and rue de Grenelle, on the site of n° 115, the adulated Adrienne Lecouvreur from the Comédie-Frangaise, is said to have been buried secretly in 1730.

script_body: The Ministry of Defence occupies what was once the Dominican convent of Saint-Joseph and the adjoining Hôtel de Brienne on rue Saint-Dominique. The convent was originally built for poor orphan girls — Madame de Montespan took great interest in it and made charitable donations, then retired there herself when Louis XIV left her for Madame de Maintenon. From 1747, the convent hosted the celebrated salon of Madame du Deffand, where all of Parisian intelligentsia and many honoured foreigners gathered. The Hôtel de Brienne passed to Lucien Bonaparte in 1802.
physical_cues: Ministry of Defence signage at 10/12 and 14 rue Saint-Dominique
source_passage: The convent was originally built for poor orphan girls... From 1747 all the Parisian intelligentsia and many honoured foreigners gathered at Madame du Deffand's celebrated salon.

script_body: Rue de Grenelle is a museum of 18th-century aristocratic Paris — but one almost entirely closed to the public. The Hôtel de Baufremont at number 87 has barely been touched by renovators and retains its original Regency harmony. The Hôtel d'Avaray at number 85 remained in the Avaray family for a remarkable 200 years, until 1896; it was bought in 1920 by the Dutch government for its Embassy. The Russian Embassy at number 79 still preserves early 18th-century decoration in its lounges and a splendid staircase. Tzar Nicholas II and his Tsarina stayed here during their 1896 Paris visit.
physical_cues: Street facades of Hôtel de Baufremont, Hôtel d'Avaray, and Russian Embassy visible from rue de Grenelle
source_passage: Hétel d' Avaray at n° 85 was built at the same time and remained in the hands of the Avaray family for a remarkable 200 years.

script_body: The Square Samuel-Rousseau across from this neo-Gothic church is dedicated to the memory of César Franck, who served as organist at Sainte-Clotilde from 1858 until his death in 1890 — over three decades at the same instrument. A sculpture of the composer meditating stands in the square, an angel hovering above symbolizing divine inspiration. Franck transformed French organ music from this church; his students included d'Indy and Chausson, and his improvisations here were legendary.
physical_cues: Sculpture of César Franck in Square Samuel-Rousseau
source_passage: the Square Samuel-Rousseau, with its colourful flower-beds, recalls the composer César Franck who, from 1858 until his death in 1890, was the organist of the church of Sainte-Clotilde.

script_body: Sainte-Clotilde is a 19th-century pastiche of Gothic architecture — built by Gau and completed by Ballu, the same architect who designed several other Parisian churches including the Trinité north of the Opéra. Unlike medieval Gothic cathedrals built over centuries, Sainte-Clotilde was conceived whole, its twin spires rising with the confident symmetry that only a Victorian-era architect would dare.
physical_cues: Twin spires dominating the rue Las Cases approach
source_passage: The church is a 19th-century pastiche of Gothic architecture, built by Gau and Ballu.

script_body: The politician who outlasted every revolution was Talleyrand — and at the Hôtel de Gallifet at 73 rue de Grenelle, he came to live not once but four times under four completely different regimes: the Directoire and into the Consulat, the First Empire, the First Restoration, and the Second Restoration after Waterloo. Napoleon, who was not fooled by this chameleon, famously defined him as 'shit in a silk stocking.' The insult stuck. The compliment was that Talleyrand kept his head.
physical_cues: Main entrance on rue de Varenne
Italian Cultural Institute signage on rue de Grenelle
source_passage: The Hotel de Gallifet at n° 73 (main entrance being on rue de Varenne), has been occupied by the Italian Embassy since 1909.

script_body: The church of the Dome — also known as the Royal Chapel — is one of the most outstanding monuments in Paris, a masterpiece of 17th-century architecture built by Jules-Hardouin Mansart. Its proportions were once seen at their best from Avenue de Breteuil on a fine morning, when the deep purple dome looked almost palpably mellow and pulpy. That patina was lost when Paris was groomed for the bicentenary of the Revolution: the dome was daubed with shiny gold paint. The regilding was executed to the highest standards, but it destroyed what only time can bestow. By night, however, the dome shimmering against the dark sky above the floodlit walls remains enchanting.
physical_cues: Look up at the golden dome
Best appreciated from Place Vauban or Pont Alexandre III
source_passage: the church of the Dome (also known as the Royal Chapel)... a masterpiece of 17th-century architecture, built by Jules-Hardouin Mansart.

script_body: It was Louis XIV, assisted by his minister Louvois, who in 1670 founded the Hôtel des Invalides. Distressed by the sight of war cripples reduced to begging on the Pont-Neuf after loyal service on the battlefield, the Sun King felt he owed them respectable shelter. The initiative had earlier roots: Henri IV in 1604 had provided shelter for veterans on the present rue Broca, and Louis XIII and Richelieu built the hospital of Bicêtre. But Louis XIV tackled the issue on a grand scale, commissioning Libéral Bruant to build a monument colossal in size — its façade measures 195 metres across and the main courtyard, the Cour d'Honneur, 102 metres by 63 — yet subdued in character. Montesquieu wrote of it: 'I believe this to be the most respectable place on earth.'
source_passage: it was Louis XIV, assisted by his minister Louvois, who in 1670 founded the Hotel des Invalides.

script_body: The veterans Louis XIV sheltered here were not easily persuaded to trade their scrappy independence on the Pont-Neuf for military discipline. And they had good reason to be alarmed: infractions were punished by anything from deprivation of wine to imprisonment, or by public humiliation astride a wooden horse. If caught with a woman of pleasure, both were exposed together for the amusement of passers-by. A complaint about poor soup once sparked a full-blown riot. Minister Louvois crushed the rebellion and had the most unruly rebel shot by a firing squad.
physical_cues: Cour d'Honneur where punishments were displayed
source_passage: a harsh military discipline was imposed... a complaint about the poor quality of the soup sparked off an outburst of violence, which soon developed into a full-blown riot.

script_body: Louvois was not a modest man and had his eye on the Invalides as his own sepulchre. Louis XIV would not tolerate such impertinence and had his remains removed elsewhere. But Louvois did find a subtle way to perpetuate his name: as you enter the Cour d'Honneur, look at the fifth garret to the right of the left-hand pavilion. Its bull's-eye window is framed by a wolf ('loup') that gazes ('voit') intensely down on the courtyard — a far-fetched pun, but one that passed unnoticed by the Sun King.
physical_cues: Fifth garret right of left-hand pavilion in Cour d'Honneur — bull's-eye window framed by carved wolf
source_passage: look at the fifth garret to the right of the left-hand side pavilion; its bull's-eye window is framed by a wolf ('loup') which looks ('voit') intensely down on to the courtyard.

script_body: Napoleon wished to be buried 'on the banks of the Seine, by the French people whom I have loved so much.' After seven years of negotiations with the English, his ashes arrived from Saint Helena on 15 December 1840, travelling via Le Havre, up the Seine to Pont de Neuilly, then down the Champs-Élysées to the Invalides through a snowstorm. Victor Hugo, who was present, described the moment the sun broke through as the hearse appeared: 'The effect was prodigious indeed.' Some 850,000 Parisians came to pay homage in the following days. Napoleon's ashes were finally moved to their permanent tomb — designed by Visconti — on 2 April 1861. He lies within six nested coffins; a silver vase holds his heart; a silver box, his stomach.
physical_cues: Circular crypt with massive red quartzite sarcophagus
Twelve allegorical figures around the tomb
source_passage: the Emperor's ashes were brought from the island of Saint Helena to the Invalides on the 15 December 1840.

script_body: The church of Saint-Louis-des-Invalides — the original church of the institution, designed by Libéral Bruant — boasts a magnificent 17th-century organ. It was here, on 5 December 1837, that Hector Berlioz's Requiem received its world premiere, performed with 188 instrumentalists and 210 choristers, at a ceremony commemorating General Damrémont, killed at the Siege of Constantine.
source_passage: The church also boasts a magnificent 17th-century organ which was used in 1837, for the first performance of Berlioz's Requiem.

script_body: Buried in the crypt of Saint-Louis-des-Invalides is Rouget de Lisle, the captain from Strasbourg who in 1792 composed 'Le Chant de guerre pour l'armée du Rhin' — the song that became La Marseillaise, France's ferociously sanguinary national anthem. His ashes were brought here on 14 July 1915, awaiting a planned transfer to the Panthéon that has never yet happened.
source_passage: Rouget de Lisle, the captain from Strasbourg who in 1792 composed Le Chant de guerre pour l'armée du Rhin... His ashes were brought here on 14 July 1915.

script_body: Napoleon was determined to stamp his own identity on the Invalides and eclipse his predecessor. In 1797 he transferred the lion of the defeated Serenissima Republic to this stronghold of French military glory, placing it atop a fountain in the centre of the Esplanade. He also hoped to bring the golden cross of the Kremlin back as a trophy and display it on the Dome — but history decided otherwise. The Venetian lion's Parisian career was brief: by 1815 it had returned to its column in Piazza San Marco.
physical_cues: Central fountain on the Esplanade des Invalides
source_passage: in 1797, had already transferred the lion of the defeated Serenissima Republic to this stronghold of France's military glory.

script_body: West of the Invalides was once a village called Le Gros Caillou — 'the big stone' — named after the boundary marker between the domains of the abbeys of Saint-Germain and Sainte-Geneviève. The village grew up to serve the 30-year construction of the Invalides: its first shop was a butcher's on rue Saint-Dominique, and the parallel rue de Grenelle accommodated laundresses who did the Invalides' washing in the Seine. Its parish church at n° 92 rue Saint-Dominique was won only after years of petitions to the King — before it, villagers had to drag all the way to Saint-Sulpice for their sacraments. The current church dates from 1822.
source_passage: The church of Saint-Pierre du Gros Caillou at n° 92 was the original parish church of the long-forgotten village.

script_body: More than any other street, pedestrian rue Cler perpetuates the village atmosphere of the old Gros Caillou neighbourhood. Its permanent market — held both mornings and afternoons — is described as the most picturesque street in the 7th arrondissement: an explosion of genuine local colour, all the more vivid for being such a contrast with the formal residential avenues surrounding it.
physical_cues: Cobblestones and market stalls between rue de Grenelle and avenue de la Motte-Picquet
source_passage: the pedestrian rue Cler... perpetuates the village atmosphere par excellence with its permanent market.

script_body: At the arcaded corner of rue Saint-Dominique and rue de l'Exposition stands La Fontaine de Mars, one of several fountains bequeathed to Paris by Napoleon. Mars, god of war, is depicted being offered water by Hygeia, goddess of health. The adjacent restaurant of the same name is one of those unpretentious places with genuine atmosphere — warm, welcoming, and serving honest traditional French cooking, a rarity in modern Paris.
physical_cues: Arcaded hemicycle at the corner; Mars's helmeted head and Hygeia with serpent
source_passage: La Fontaine de Mars, one of several bequeathed to Paris by Napoleon. Mars, the god of war, is depicted being offered water by the goddess of health, Hygeia.

script_body: At n° 29 Avenue Rapp stands an astonishing building by Jules Lavirotte, built in 1901 and frequently compared to the work of Antoni Gaudí. It is one of the finest surviving examples of Art Nouveau in Paris, its façade lavished with ceramic sculpture — flowers, animals, bison heads supporting balconies, fox-headed fur collars — and awarded the prize for the most original new façade in the 7th arrondissement that year.
source_passage: At n° 29 is an astonishing building, built by Lavirotte and extremely reminiscent of the work of the Spanish architect, Gaudf.

script_body: Just as Madame de Maintenon founded the school of Saint-Cyr for the children of the impoverished nobility, Madame de Pompadour founded the École Militaire to enable impoverished young men to become officers. She instructed Gabriel — who had already impressed the court with his Petit Trianon at Versailles — to design this new academy. Among the cadets who later paraded on the adjacent Champ de Mars was a poor Corsican who would one day inspect and distribute honours to the troops there.
physical_cues: Grand classical façade facing Place de Fontenoy
source_passage: Madame de Pompadour founded the Ecole Militaire to enable impoverished young men to become officers... instructed Gabriel.

script_body: On Place de Fontenoy, facing the west wing of the École Militaire, stands the UNESCO building, designed jointly by Marcel Breuer (US), Pier Luigi Nervi (Italy) and Bernard Zehrfuss (France), and inaugurated in 1958. Its Y-shaped form was quite revolutionary when it was designed, and, like all good architecture, remains effective today. Outside stand works by Calder, Miró, and Moore; inside, by Picasso, Arp, Braque, Miró, and others. The Japanese garden was designed by the sculptor Isamu Noguchi, who returned to Paris to restore it in 1988, shortly before his death.
physical_cues: Y-shaped concrete structure visible from Place de Fontenoy
source_passage: the UNESCO building, designed jointly by Marcel Breuer (US), Pietro Nervi (Italy) and Bernard Zehrfuss (France).

script_body: The Champ de Mars was the stage for the earliest experiments in flight. On 27 August 1783, the physicist J. A. C. Charles and the Robert brothers released the world's first unmanned hydrogen balloon from here — a 35-cubic-metre sphere of rubberised silk that flew 15 miles in three-quarters of an hour. The people of Gonesse, east of Paris, were panic-stricken when it descended on them from the heavens. Then on 2 March 1784, Jean-Pierre Blanchard brought his sophisticated balloon equipped with four oars and a rudder — it was meant to float northeast to La Villette but headed stubbornly west to Billancourt, to the delight of the chansonniers. Undaunted, Blanchard went on to make the first aerial crossing of the English Channel from Dover to Calais in January 1785, together with American John Jeffries.
physical_cues: Flat open field — original launchpad for ballooning
source_passage: on 27 August, the Roberts released this first unmanned hydrogen balloon from the Champ-de-Mars.

script_body: In 1863 the photographer Nadar took off from the Champ de Mars in a huge balloon called Le Géant, accompanied by prominent figures, in a nacelle styled as a two-storey wicker house. On his second flight the balloon crashed in Hanover, Germany, injuring Nadar.
physical_cues: Site of Le Géant's first launch on 4 October 1863
source_passage: In 1863 the photographer Nadar took off from the Champ-de-Mars... in a huge balloon with a double-decker nacelle, called Le Géant.

script_body: The authorities of the Revolution chose the Champ de Mars as the site for the first Bastille Day celebrations — La Fête de la Fédération — on 14 July 1790, presided over by Talleyrand. 300,000 fervent patriots, including the Royal Family, gathered here; La Fayette, standing in the pouring rain, took the Nation's oath, the first citizen to do so. By 1793 the Terror had arrived: the guillotine was briefly erected here to execute the hated Bailly — former President of the Constituent Assembly and Mayor of Paris — who waited stoically while the blood-thirsty crowd covered him in spittle and mud.
physical_cues: Vast open axis from Ecole Militaire to Eiffel Tower
source_passage: 300,000 fervent patriots - including the Royal Family - were convened here on that 14 July 1790.

script_body: From 1855 the Champ de Mars became the playground of the emerging capitalist age — the site of successive Expositions Universelles where French technological achievements dazzled the world.
