The 1889 fair featured the Galerie des Machines (420 × 115 metres, 16,000 machines) and the just-completed Eiffel Tower rising 300 metres — never before had mortal eye embraced such horizons except from a balloon. In 1900, an electrically operated moving wooden platform transported visitors from the Champ de Mars to the Champs-Élysées and back, electricity still being a luxury. The age of Universal Exhibitions has gone, an ephemeral spark fizzled out by ennui before being swept away by universal cataclysms.
physical_cues: Vast plain that hosted temporary exhibition halls
source_passage: in 1855 the Champ-de-Mars was singled out to become the gigantic playground of the emerging capitalist society.

corrections.original: Eiffel Tower towering 318 metres above Paris
corrections.corrected: Original height 300m without antenna (1889); 330m today including antenna

script_body: How ironic to recall that 300 prominent members of the intelligentsia signed a petition against the Eiffel Tower's erection, calling it a crime against history and against Paris. Yet it survived its planned demolition and became the unassailable emblem of the city. Even visitors familiar with skyscrapers feel overwhelmed as they approach it: 18,038 metal pieces held together by 2.5 million rivets weighing 7,300 tonnes — an extraordinary technological feat.
physical_cues: Lattice of iron visible in daylight
source_passage: 300 prominent members of the intelligentsia of the time signed a petition against its erection.

script_body: The Tower has attracted both the heroic and the desperate. Eccentrics attempted to fly from it with homemade wings — an Austrian called Reichelt in 1912 hit the ground head first. In 1977 a French stunt man flew a hang-glider from the first floor; an English couple parachuted from the third; an American pilot flew between its legs and lost his licence. Of the 380 people who have hurled themselves from the Tower, only one escaped death — a young woman in 1964 who landed on the roof of a parked car. That year suicides averaged one per month, after which parapets were installed.
physical_cues: Safety parapets and mesh added after 1964
source_passage: Of the 380 people who have hurled themselves from the Tower, only one escaped death - a young woman who in 1964 jumped from the first floor but landed on the roof of a parked car.

script_body: During World War I, the Eiffel Tower played a crucial military role: Mata Hari, the infamous dancer-spy, was identified through radio transmissions intercepted at the Tower's wireless station. Coded messages sent by a German contact referred to agent 'H21' — swiftly identified as Mata Hari. She was captured and shot on 15 October 1917. Nearly 50,000 words were received and transmitted from the Tower during that war — alone a compelling reason not to demolish it.
physical_cues: Antenna at the summit — descendant of WWI radio mast
source_passage: Identified through its radio transmissions as H21, she was captured and shot on 15 October 1917.

script_body: An event of great novelty occurred on the Champ de Mars one fine morning in 1780: two gentlemen ran a horse-race for a bet, the first of a series of sports imported from England that became fashionable in Paris throughout the 19th century. Marie-Antoinette gave enthusiastic support; even the Revolution adopted horse-racing, though the jockeys of those 'patriotic horse-races of public utility' wore tricoloured sashes. The Champ de Mars remained Paris's racecourse until 1855, when Longchamp in the Bois de Boulogne took over.
physical_cues: Long flat expanse — nearly 800m from Ecole Militaire to Eiffel Tower
source_passage: An event of great novelty occurred here one fine morning in 1780, when two gentlemen ran in a horse-race for a bet.

script_body: Marie Curie lived at 36 quai de Bethune from 1912 to 1934. Nearby, the cosmetics magnate Helena Rubinstein purchased a Le Vau mansion in 1932 — and to the horror of preservationists, demolished it in 1935 to build a modernist replacement.

The Hotel de Lauzun was built by architect Charles Chamois and features some of the most lavishly decorated interiors in Paris. The Duc de Lauzun, who gave the mansion its name, led a turbulent life — he secretly married the Grande Mademoiselle (Louis XIV's cousin) and was imprisoned in the fortress of Pignerol for his audacity.

Place de Greve hosted the fete de la Saint-Jean on 24 June, when a 10-metre-high bonfire celebrated the birth of John the Baptist. Occasionally the King himself would come to light the fire, heralded by trumpets.

Place Royale was a favourite site for duels, watched from balconies by ladies whose favours were being sought. Cardinal Richelieu banned duels in 1626. When Boutteville contravened the ruling, believing his glorious pedigree put him above the law, Richelieu had him decapitated at Place de Greve.

Parisians, never short of a cutting nickname, dubbed the Centre Pompidou 'Notre-Dame-des-Tuyaux' — Our Lady of the Pipes. The irreverent name captures both the outrage and the grudging affection Parisians developed for the building's industrial aesthetic in the heart of their historic city.

At 36 rue des Tournelles, just steps from this square, the legendary Ninon Lenclos held court in a modest house where Molière, Boileau, La Fontaine and the Duc d'Orléans brought their own food in recognition of their hosts' slender means. Ninon transformed what in others was scandalous prostitution into a socially acceptable way of life — 'the triumph of vice conducted with wit,' as Saint-Simon put it. She was irresistible to the greatest men of France, welcoming them all into her generous bed. The puritanical Anne of Austria eventually had her locked up in the Madelonnettes, a convent-prison for repentant prostitutes — despite Ninon's famous protest that she was 'neither a whore nor repentant.' Undaunted, she ate ostentatiously during Lent and threw her meat bone out the window — a brave act when impiety was punishable by death.

The Hotel-Dieu is the oldest hospital in Paris, founded in the 12th century by Maurice de Sully, the same bishop who initiated the construction of Notre-Dame. For centuries it was the only hospital serving the city, and conditions were appalling — up to five patients were crammed into a single bed.

At number 254, the parish church of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs beautifully illustrates the evolution from Gothic to Renaissance. Its picturesque tower dates largely to the early 15th century, and the Renaissance portal on the south side survives as a fine example of the transition between styles.

Inside the old church of Saint-Martin, the Musee National des Techniques offers one of Paris's most underrated displays. Follow humanity's technological adventure through the centuries — from the sundial to satellites, from the first standard units for measures and weights to early recordings and early cinema, from steam engines to Bleriot's aircraft, with which he became the first person to cross the English Channel in 1909. The Gothic dining hall, now the library of the Conservatoire, is a masterpiece of ethereal lightness.

Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano designed the Centre Georges Pompidou with bright blue building and bright red and blue piping. Parisians were scandalized that two 'hippy' architects built a 'refinery' in the historic heart of Paris — twenty years later it still ranked first among monuments they wished to see wiped out. Yet it drew 28,000 visitors per day and 8 million per year, beating the Eiffel Tower's 2.5 million.

The old Pont au Double, which connected the Hotel-Dieu to the Left Bank, featured an enclosed glass gallery where recovering patients could promenade — an early form of therapeutic architecture, allowing the sick to take the air without leaving the hospital.

The Hotel de Sens is one of the oldest civilian monuments in Paris. Its most dramatic episode came in 1606, when the ageing Queen Margot — Henri IV's first wife — was living here. As her coach was leaving, the Comte de Vermond shot dead a rival lover on the very threshold. Margot, enraged, had Vermond arrested, and he was beheaded the following day in front of the hotel.

Where this peaceful garden now stands, the Knights Templar once ruled a fortified city-within-a-city. Organised as a fighting order in the Holy Land in 1118, the Templars settled on the eastern edge of Paris around 1139 and spent a century draining the surrounding marshland — the 'marais' that gave this district its name. Behind crenellated walls and watchtowers, they ran a kind of international deposit bank, growing fabulously wealthy. But Philippe le Bel, himself chronically short of funds, could not tolerate this state within his state. After taking shelter with the Templars during a riot in 1306 and witnessing their stupendous riches first-hand, he contrived their destruction through false accusations and torture. The Order was suppressed in 1312 and on 18 March 1314, their last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, was burned at the stake on the Ile aux Juifs — now the tip of Place Dauphine — where he thundered out prophecies of doom for the King and Pope. Both died that same year.

The Hôtel Carnavalet is the third oldest non-religious monument in Paris, after the Hôtel de Sens and the Hôtel de Cluny. Built around 1548 for Jacques des Ligneris, President of Parliament, it owes its gorgeous bas-relief of the Seasons in the courtyard to Jean Goujon, the King's official sculptor. Its architecture — ornate Italian Renaissance blended with French formality — is characteristic of the reign of François I, who sought to bridge two cultures after his Italian campaigns. Coysevox's statue of the Sun King in the courtyard, miraculously rescued during the Revolution, was transferred here from the Hôtel de Ville.

Rue des Rosiers is the backbone of the pletzel — Yiddish for 'little square' — the historic Jewish quarter of the Marais. At number 20 stood the Hotel des Juifs, a reminder of the community's deep roots here. The street's most heartbreaking memorial marks the deportation of 165 pupils from a local school during the Occupation — children who never returned.

The anti-bourgeois proletarian Commune burnt down the Hotel de Ville in 1871. The victorious bourgeois government of the Third Republic rebuilt it at once in its old style, to brush off this incident and demonstrate that its possession was irrevocable.

poi_name: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
script_body: At the eastern tip of the Ile de la Cite, steps descend into a stark underground crypt — the Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation. The narrow entrance forces visitors into single file, evoking the claustrophobia of deportation. The poet Robert Desnos, who had been active in the Resistance, died at the Theresienstadt concentration camp just weeks before liberation.

The Jesuits arrived in Paris in 1580 and established themselves on rue Saint-Antoine. Louis XIII laid the cornerstone of this church in 1627, and Cardinal Richelieu celebrated its first mass in 1641. The imposing baroque facade, unusual for Paris, reflects the Counter-Reformation confidence of the Jesuit order.

Notre-Dame endured centuries of vandalism before the Revolution even began. The medieval chancel screen was destroyed in 1699 to make way for a more fashionable baroque interior. The original stained glass windows — except for the three great rose windows — were ripped out and replaced with plain white glass to 'let in more light.'

Eugene Viollet-le-Duc began his controversial restoration of Notre-Dame in 1844, guided by his famous principle: 'To restore a building is not to maintain it, repair it, or rebuild it; it is to re-establish it in a complete state which may never have existed at any given moment.' He added the spire, the gargoyles, and much of what the world came to think of as 'original' medieval decoration.

The Hotel Lamoignon was built for Diane de France, the illegitimate daughter of Henri II and a Piedmontese woman. Later, President Lamoignon established a literary academy here that attracted Racine, Boileau, and Madame de Sevigne. It was also the site of the trial of the notorious poisoner La Brinvilliers, whose crimes horrified 17th-century Paris.

Before Catherine Bellier's time, this site held the house of Marie Touchet, mistress of Charles IX. She bore the king his only surviving son — a child who, had legitimacy not been an obstacle, could have changed the entire line of French succession and perhaps averted the Wars of Religion.

The Marais in its golden age was studded with magnificent hotels. Great architects Mansart and Le Vau and painters Le Brun, Mignard and Vouet decorated the interiors. The Duc de Richelieu sold ten Nicolas Poussin paintings to Louis XIV and bought some twenty Rubens to replace them.

The municipality of Paris grew from the corporation of water merchants who bought the strand (greve) from Louis VII in the 12th century. A tribunal of commerce was set up on Place de Greve, becoming the embryo of the municipality. The corporation's seal, inherited from the ancient Nautae Parisiaci, remains the coat of arms of Paris with only minor changes a thousand years later.

This is the only religious building ever designed by Hector Guimard, the Art Nouveau architect famous for his Paris Metro entrances. Its undulating facade in concrete is unmistakably Guimard. He married an American heiress, Miss Oppenheimer, suggesting a personal connection to the Jewish community that may have inspired this commission.

The church of Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis was the stage for some of the greatest preaching and music of the 17th century. Marc-Antoine Charpentier composed his celebrated Miserere for these acoustics. The Jesuit preacher Bourdaloue was so popular that ladies would arrive six hours early to secure a seat — they even had a special hat named after him, designed to be worn during his lengthy sermons.

The Pavillon du Roi dominates the south side of the square, grander than the other 36 houses that form the harmonious ensemble. The square was inaugurated in 1612 with a spectacular three-day celebration for the double wedding of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, and his sister Elisabeth with the future Philip IV of Spain. It was renamed Place des Vosges in 1800, honouring the first department to pay its taxes to the new Republic.

Saint-Gervais-Saint-Protais has origins reaching back to the 6th century, making it one of the oldest parish churches in Paris. Its west facade, completed in 1621, was the first in Paris to use the classical orders — Doric on the ground floor, Ionic above, and Corinthian at the top — a formula that would be widely imitated. Voltaire remarked that it was 'the most beautiful thing of its kind in France.'

Between rue Vertbois, rue Volta and rue des Fontaines-du-Temple stood the vast Convent of the Madelonnettes, built in 1618 to save the souls of 'fallen women.' The most notorious inmate was Ninon de Lenclos, imprisoned by Anne of Austria to quell the commotion she caused among the court's great men. She protested she was 'neither a whore nor repented.' When her suitors threatened to burn the place down, patrols circled every night until she was removed to a convent in Lagny. When the building was demolished in 1865, skeletons were found under a trap-door behind a church pillar — rebellious detainees apparently left to die.

The Village Saint-Paul is a warren of interconnected courtyards filled with antique dealers and curiosity shops. It takes its name from a 7th-century church that once stood here — one of the oldest in Paris — which was destroyed by the Norsemen during their devastating raids on the city.

The Parisians nicknamed this showy mansion 'l'hôtel salé' — the salty hotel — because its builder, Aubert de Fontenay, had made his fortune collecting the salt tax. But 'salé' in colloquial French also means expensive, and Aubert, said to have started out as a lackey, went all out to impress: Corinthian pillars, medallions, sculpted eagles, a fabulous wrought-iron balustrade marked with his initials and those of his wealthy wife Mademoiselle Chastelain — who helped him rise in the world but also made him a cuckold. Like many parvenus, he lost everything in the wake of Fouquet's downfall and died before his masterpiece was completed. When a century later the Archbishop of Paris acquired it, he laid a crimson carpet on the gorgeous staircase and covered up the nude sculptures on the walls.

The church holds notable burials: Mademoiselle de Scudery, the celebrated novelist who died in 1701 aged 93; Guillaume de Bude, founder of the College de France, who died in 1540; and members of the La Bruyere and Ormesson families. The renowned 18th-century actor Talma was baptized here.

Beaumarchais lived in this magnificent mansion from 1776 and wrote Le Mariage de Figaro here — the play that scandalised the aristocracy and foreshadowed the Revolution. But he was also a secret agent: from this very address he set up a front company to supply arms and ammunition to the American revolutionaries fighting for independence from Britain, with the tacit approval of Louis XVI.
With the court's transfer to Versailles in 1682, the Marais declined. In 1962, Andre Malraux's rehabilitation bill passed; in 1965 the area was declared a protected zone.

Across from the Arsenal library stands the Pavillon de l'Arsenal, a 19th-century glass and steel structure that served as an art gallery and later as a warehouse of the Samaritaine department store. Since 1988 it has housed temporary exhibitions on different aspects of town planning in Paris.

The cloister adjoining the church, built in 1427, is the only surviving medieval cloister in Paris. The church itself is now Protestant — a historical irony given its origins in anti-Jewish persecution under the Catholic Church.

In the early 18th century, Voltaire was beaten up by the lackeys of the Prince de Rohan near the Hotel de Sully. The young writer challenged the prince to a duel, but Rohan's aristocratic family had Voltaire thrown into the Bastille instead. Upon his release, Voltaire left for England — an exile that would profoundly shape his political philosophy and produce his influential Letters on the English.

On this site stood La Force prison, the scene of one of the Revolution's most horrifying episodes. In September 1792, during the massacres, the Princesse de Lamballe — Marie-Antoinette's closest friend — was dragged from her cell and murdered by the mob. Her head was impaled on a pike and paraded to the Temple prison, where it was thrust before the windows of the captive Queen.

The Stravinsky Fountain, inaugurated in 1983, is a collaboration between Jean Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle. Tinguely's black mechanical sculptures spray and spin alongside Saint Phalle's colourful, voluptuous figures — a joyful pop-art homage to the compositions of Igor Stravinsky, including The Firebird and The Rite of Spring.

Henri IV dreamed of making Paris a centre of silk manufacture, hoping to rival Lyon and undercut costly Italian imports. He brought 200 Italian workers to the site of this square and planted mulberry trees for their silkworms. But the northern climate defeated the enterprise — the silkworms simply could not survive Parisian winters, and the project was abandoned.

Place Royale (now Place des Vosges) was the first open-air square in Paris. Its exquisite bright pink brick and white stone pavilions served in 1612 as the backdrop for the most dazzling celebration recalled by Parisians: the double wedding of Louis XIII and his sister Elisabeth.

The Visitandine convent was a fashionable retreat for society women tired of worldly life. Madame de La Fayette, author of La Princesse de Cleves, retired here as Soeur Angelique. But not all residents took to piety: the tempestuous Hortense Mancini, niece of Cardinal Mazarin, once poured black ink into the holy water font.

At number 3 rue Volta, an astonishing sight: a medieval half-timbered house shared by a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese hairstylist. For decades this was proclaimed the oldest house in Paris, supposedly dating to the late 13th century. This tiny Chinatown around rues Volta, Le Maire and Gravilliers is the oldest Chinese community in Paris, descended from immigrants who arrived during World War I.

The quai des Balcons earned its name from the series of ornate iron balconies lining its facades. The 18th-century writer Mercier observed that the island had 'its own moral code, its own customs' — a village within Paris that to this day retains an insular, self-contained atmosphere quite unlike the rest of the city.

The Memorial de la Shoah began as the Memorial to the Unknown Jewish Martyr, built in 1956. An eternal flame burns in the crypt, and the Wall of Names records the 75,000 Jews — men, women and children — deported from France to the Nazi death camps. Only 2,500 returned.

In Rabelais's tale, the giant Gargantua visited Notre-Dame and, followed and gawked at by Parisians, climbed the church tower and urinated on the crowd below, drowning 260,418 people (exclusive of women and children). In Rabelais's version, the city of Lutetia became known as Paris — from 'par rie' (for a laugh) — in recognition of Gargantua's jest.

On Good Friday 1918, a German long-range shell from the infamous Big Bertha cannon struck the church during a service, bringing the roof crashing down on the congregation. Eighty-eight people were killed and sixty-eight wounded — one of the worst single attacks on civilians in Paris during the Great War.

Victor Hugo's 1831 novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame was written partly as a plea to save the crumbling cathedral. The book ignited a wave of public passion for the medieval monument and directly led to the campaign for its restoration — proof that a novel can save a building.

Look up. Every rivet you see was placed by hand — 2.5 million of them. Gustave Eiffel didn't build this for beauty; he built it to prove iron could touch the sky. Parisians called it an eyesore. Now it's the most visited paid monument on Earth.

Hugo's domestic life at Place des Vosges was turbulent. His wife Adele carried on an affair with their close friend, the critic Sainte-Beuve. Hugo himself began a passionate liaison with the actress Juliette Drouet, who lived nearby. A secret back staircase allowed discreet comings and goings — the arrangement lasted for fifty years until Drouet's death.

The BHV began when Xavier Ruel conducted one of Paris's first market surveys, standing outside the Hotel de Ville counting passersby. Convinced by the foot traffic, he opened a shop specialising in screws, nails and household hardware — a focus the store maintains to this day in its legendary basement. Originally called the Bazar Parisien, it was renamed after Napoleon III fell from power.

Notre-Dame hosted only two coronations, both controversial: Henry VI of England, who had conquered France, and Emperor Napoleon. The legitimate French dynasties always used the cathedral of Reims. Henri IV's conversion to Catholicism was celebrated here in 1593 with a Te Deum, though the conversion ceremony itself took place at Saint-Denis.

The Bastille was far from the grim dungeon of popular imagination. It functioned as a luxury prison for well-connected inmates. Voltaire completed his tragedy Oedipe here, composing verses and dining well. The Marquis de Sade draped his cell walls with fabric and had his own furniture brought in. When the fortress was finally stormed on July 14, 1789, the liberators found only seven prisoners inside — a far cry from the hundreds the revolutionaries imagined they would free.

In 1766, the ten-year-old Mozart was brought to this very spot — then the glittering court of the Prince de Conti — on his second visit to Paris. The Grand Prior's Palace, built by Mansart in 1667, had become a free-thinking alternative court where 'gathered those who had nothing to hope for from the King,' as Horace Walpole noted. Mozart played the harpsichord in the drawing-room to a largely inattentive audience — a scene immortalised in Ollivier's famous painting. The Temple's brilliant social life masked a shallow artistic commitment. Earlier, the Prince had appointed the abbé Prévost, author of Manon Lescaut, as chaplain — unbothered that the clergyman never celebrated mass. When Prévost pointed this out, Conti retorted: 'It is of little consequence — I never listen to it.'

Guillaume Apollinaire lived at 43 quai de Bourbon, where he and the painter Marie Laurencin carried on their celebrated love affair. The building was known as the Maison du Centaure — a fitting address for the poet who championed Cubism and coined the term 'surrealism.'

Sylvia Beach opened the original shop in 1919 and published Ulysses when no one else would. This reincarnation, opened by George Whitman in 1951, still lets writers sleep among the shelves — they call them Tumbleweeds.

poi_name: Crypte Archeologique de l'Ile de la Cite
script_body: Beneath the parvis of Notre-Dame lies an underground museum revealing the layers of Paris's past. The archaeological crypt displays remains of ancient Lutetia — Gallo-Roman walls, a quay, a hypocaust heating system, and medieval cellars — two thousand years of history directly beneath your feet.

The Centre Pompidou's piazza became a focal point of Parisian street life, with buskers, acrobats, mime artists, jugglers, fire-eaters, portrait painters and pickpockets spontaneously recreating the medieval atmosphere of the parvis of Notre-Dame.

Built in the 14th century for ammunition manufacture, the Arsenal lay along an arm of the Seine (now Boulevard Morland). In 1563 a gigantic explosion — heard as far as Melun, 46 km away — blew most of it up. The Duc de Sully built a palatial residence there. Louis XIV later used the abandoned foundry to cast bronze statues for the gardens of Versailles.

The Hotel de Sully was built in 1624 for Mesme Gallet, a notorious gambler who squandered his fortune on a single night's losses and had to sell up. The aged Duc de Sully bought it next, but his young wife's infidelities were legendary. The pragmatic duke installed a separate staircase so her lovers could come and go without crossing his path.

Charles Baudelaire lived in a small apartment at the Hotel de Lauzun from 1843, where he began composing Les Fleurs du Mal. Theophile Gautier founded the Club des Haschichins here, and the literary elite gathered to experiment with hashish — evenings that Baudelaire later chronicled in his Artificial Paradises.

In the 14th century, the painter Jacquemin Gringonneur lived on this street and was commissioned to paint playing cards for the amusement of Charles VI, the mad king. Legend has it that the King of Hearts was modelled on Charles VI himself — a fitting tribute to a monarch whose bouts of insanity plunged France into chaos.

The church of Saint-Merri, built from 1520, is a fine example of flamboyant Gothic — one of the last Gothic churches in Paris, built when the Renaissance had already arrived. Its bell, cast in 1331, is the oldest in Paris, having survived revolutions, wars and the great foundry melts that claimed most medieval bells.

The Arsenal housed the court of justice where the trial of Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's treasurer, was held in 1664. Despite Colbert's rigged magistrates, the courageous d'Ormesson defied the King's wish for a death sentence and voted for banishment. Louis XIV then commuted the sentence upward to life imprisonment.

Victor Hugo moved to this apartment at 6 Place des Vosges in 1832 and lived here for sixteen years. In these rooms he wrote the drama Ruy Blas and sketched out the early plans for his masterwork Les Miserables. The apartment preserves his furniture and many of his own drawings and decorative pieces.

The sculptor Camille Claudel had her studio on the quai de Bourbon from 1899 to 1913. These were her final years of creative freedom before she was committed to a psychiatric institution by her family, where she remained for the last thirty years of her life — one of the most tragic stories in the history of art.

The monks of Saint-Martin played a major role in developing this part of Paris, shaping its streets and economy over centuries. They were also associated with some of France's most powerful churchmen — including Cardinal de Richelieu, the mastermind behind the centralization of French royal power under Louis XIII.

The Couperin dynasty held the post of organist at Saint-Gervais for an extraordinary 173 years, from 1653 to 1826. The most famous, Francois Couperin 'le Grand,' was appointed at the age of eighteen and became the finest keyboard composer of the French Baroque.

The crenellated wall you see across the street is a surviving section of the 13th-century fortifications of the Priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, one of medieval Paris's most powerful monasteries. Notice the watch-tower with its distinctive pepper-box slate roof. It owes its survival to Victor Hugo, who fired off a letter of protest declaring: 'Demolish the tower — no; the architect — yes!' The tower was restored that very year, along with the pretty 18th-century fountain beside it. The priory church itself boasts the first example of Gothic rib vaults in the capital, though the chapel windows with their semi-circular vaults remain Romanesque — a rare blend of the two styles in one building.

Rue Saint-Martin, on which the church stands, follows the ancient Roman road that ran north from Lutetia. This was the main artery linking the Roman settlement to the northern provinces, and it remains one of the oldest continuously used streets in Paris.

Henri IV's plan for the first open-air square in Paris was carried through to completion after his death. Inaugurated to celebrate the double betrothal of Louis XIII to Anne of Austria and of his sister Elizabeth to the future Philip IV of Spain, the festivities began on 5 April 1612 and lasted three days: an extraordinary carousel of trumpets, oboes and violins paraded round the square, while the guns of the Bastille roared in the distance. At night, a torchlight procession wound through the streets of Paris and fireworks blazed over the Bastille. These events elevated the Marais to the undisputed aristocratic centre of 17th-century Paris.

Notre-Dame was the birthplace of polyphonic music in Europe. In the 12th and 13th centuries, the composers Leonin and Perotin developed the art of organum — music in multiple voices — at the cathedral's choir school. Their innovations laid the foundations for all Western harmony.

Behind this museum once stood the Théâtre du Marais, where in January 1637, Corneille's Le Cid electrified all of Paris. 'Tout Paris pour Chimène a les yeux de Rodrigue' — all Paris gazes at Chimène with the eyes of Rodrigue — wrote Boileau. But the soaring success was clouded by tragedy the following August, when the lead actor Mondory was struck by apoplexy on stage, leaving his arm and tongue permanently paralysed. The theatre survived and thrived: its new director pioneered the first special effects in Paris — Mercury descending from a star-studded sky, Jupiter hurling lightning bolts. In 1661, La Toison d'Or became the theatrical event of the century: Louis XIV himself travelled twice from the Louvre to rue Vieille-du-Temple to attend. But in 1673, after Molière's death, the jealous court musician Lully prevailed on the King to shut the theatre down.

During the Occupation, Café de Flore became an unlikely resistance hub. The Nazis preferred the Deux Magots next door — which made Flore the place where intellectuals quietly planned acts of cultural defiance.

This was the stronghold of the Guise, the greatest family of the Marais, second only to the King's. Henri I de Guise — 'le Balafré,' Scarface — hoped to seize the throne itself. He started by respectfully greeting the humblest Parisians, 'down to picklocks and fishwives,' who in return sported green scarves, the colour of House Guise. He then instigated the massacre of Saint-Bartholomew in August 1572 and plotted the overthrow of Henri III. But the King pre-empted him: on 23 December 1588, Guise was lured to the Château de Blois and assassinated. The family's wealth was staggering: Henri II de Guise owned nine abbeys by the age of eleven and was appointed Archbishop of Reims at fifteen. Madame de Sévigné described one of their balls where 'all the courtyards were lit with two thousand lanterns.' The death of the last Guise in 1696 marked the beginning of the Marais's decline.

The Porte Saint-Martin stands on the ancient Roman road from Lutetia to the north. This triumphal arch was built by Louis XIV to celebrate his victories over the Franche-Comte, the Germans, the Spanish and the Dutch. Walk up close and you'll see the sculpted figure of the Sun King in the nude as an invincible, muscular Hercules — but bewigged as always. Louis XV passed under it returning from Flanders, Napoleon after Austerlitz, and the Allied armies after Waterloo. When the city's focal point shifted westward, the Arc de Triomphe on the Champs-Elysees replaced it as Paris's symbolic ceremonial arch.

The Centre Pompidou was conceived as a transparent cultural centre for the people — a place where the inner workings of the building would be visible from the outside. The architects turned architecture inside out, placing all the structural elements, ducts, and escalators on the exterior, leaving the interior as open, flexible exhibition space.

In 1578, a savage duel took place near this mansion. Quelus, one of Henri III's favourites, was stabbed eighteen times. The distraught King ordered straw laid on the street to muffle passing carriages so his dying companion could rest in peace. The Hotel de Mayenne later became a centre for the Catholic League, and within these walls the assassination of Henri III was plotted.

The Enclos du Temple was a free zone, home to tax-exempt tradesmen, franchised craftsmen and insolvent debtors — some 4,000 people in all. Charlatan doctors practised here with impunity, and Parisians flocked to buy the Temple's herb-tea for constipation. In the 17th century, Sieur Darce began manufacturing imitation jewellery — a trade forbidden everywhere else in the kingdom. The Temple became the birthplace of fancy goods and fashion accessories, for the first time available to the masses. A vivid working-class jargon was born here too: 'chineur' for secondhand dealer and 'gonzesse' for a young woman both entered French dictionaries from the market stalls of the Temple.

Beneath Notre-Dame's chancel, vestiges of a pillar-shaped monument dedicated to Jupiter were found in 1711 — the Pilier des Nautes, erected by the corporation of water merchants (Nautae Parisiaci). Inscriptions date it to the reign of Emperor Tiberius (AD 14-37), making it the oldest sculpted monument found in the capital. The merchants engraved their own gods alongside those of Rome. The pillar is now displayed in the Musee National du Moyen Age at the Hotel de Cluny.

The Tunisian-born designer Azzedine Alaia made his home and studio at 18 rue de la Verrerie, choosing to stay in the Marais when the fashion world migrated to the Right Bank and beyond. His foundation preserves the spirit of a designer who refused to follow trends or show on the official calendar.

On the night of 23 November 1407, just steps from here, eighteen hired killers armed with hatchets and pointed mallets lay in wait on rue Vieille-du-Temple. The Duc d'Orléans — brother of the mentally impaired Charles VI, and lover of Queen Isabeau — had been lured from her side by a false summons from the King. As he rode past on his mule, the assassins hurled themselves upon him. 'I am the Duke of Orléans!' he cried, believing it a mistake. 'Precisely so. You are the man we want.' A shoemaker's wife, watching from a top-floor window, screamed 'Murder! Murder!' — but too late. The butchered Duke lay in a puddle of blood. Two days later, his cousin Jean sans Peur, Duc de Bourgogne, admitted the crime — then unleashed a civil war that would open the gates of France to English invasion.

The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789 became the founding myth of the French Revolution, yet the reality was far less dramatic. Finance minister Necker had already drawn up plans to demolish the fortress. When the mob broke in, they found only seven bewildered prisoners — four forgers, two madmen, and a young nobleman imprisoned at his family's request.

Berthillon has been serving what many consider the finest ice cream in Paris from its shop at the western tip of the Ile Saint-Louis, with Notre-Dame Cathedral as its backdrop. The queues that snake along rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Ile are a Parisian institution in their own right.

Catherine Bellier, known as 'Cateau la Borgnesse' (One-Eyed Kate), was a lady-in-waiting to Anne of Austria. She was entrusted with initiating the young Louis XIV into the ways of love. As her reward, she received the means to build this magnificent mansion, partly constructed with stones pilfered from the demolition of the old Louvre.

Just around the corner, on the intersection of rue de Beauce and rue des Oiseaux, the enlightened Mademoiselle de Scudéry held one of the most sought-after salons of the 17th century. Every Saturday, men in cascading wigs and feathered hats and women with pyramid-like headdresses would climb the dark staircase to her 'muffled, obscure sanctuary.' Her garden was a gem — acacias and fruit trees whose exquisite fragrances masked the stench of the street. A warbler, a wren and a parrot lived among the branches, and the great philosopher Leibniz solemnly addressed the parrot in verse. Ninon Lenclos, having skimmed Scudéry's preposterous Carte du Tendre — a map of platonic love — dismissed the salon members as 'the Jansenists of Love: they talk about it endlessly but never make it.'

Charles Nodier, head of the library from 1824 to 1844, gathered the Romantic writers Victor Hugo, Lamartine, Alfred de Musset, Alexandre Dumas and Sainte-Beuve, perpetuating a 200-year Parisian tradition of salons litteraires.

On September 8, 1656, Christina of Sweden made a spectacular entry into the square. The former queen, who had abdicated her throne two years earlier, arrived in Paris amid great fanfare and was received with elaborate ceremony at Place Royale.

This small church boasts one of Paris's most influential domes. Francois Mansart designed it with a circular plan and a striking 35-metre dome that became the model for two of France's greatest buildings: the Val-de-Grace and the Invalides. Napoleon gave the church to the Protestants in 1803, and it has served as a Reformed temple ever since.

The restaurant Nos Ancetres les Gaulois on the island offers a distinctive dining experience — a ribald celebration of Gallic excess with unlimited wine and rustic fare, echoing the spirit of the Gauls who once inhabited this stretch of the Seine.

The mathematician and philosopher Jean le Rond d'Alembert was found as a newborn on the steps of the church of Saint-Jean-le-Rond — which once stood near here — on 16 November 1717. A foundling abandoned by his mother, he was raised by a glazier's wife and went on to co-edit the Encyclopedie with Diderot, becoming one of the towering intellects of the Enlightenment.

The Hotel de Bretonvilliers, once the most splendid mansion on the island, was destroyed — a casualty of the same forces of modernisation and neglect that threatened the entire Marais before its 20th-century rehabilitation.

Notre-Dame's great bell, known today as Emmanuel, has a dramatic history. The original bell, called Jacqueline, was recast in 1680 and renamed Emmanuel. According to tradition, the ladies of the court threw their jewellery into the molten metal, which is said to give the bell its exceptionally pure tone.

Philippe-Auguste confiscated the Jews' possessions, using the proceeds partly to finance Les Halles market, and expelled them from France in 1182. Their centuries-old presence on rue de la Juiverie, the central axis of the Ile de la Cite, came to an end. When he invited the Jews back 16 years later to squeeze them dry once more, they settled on the right bank around rue des Rosiers.

Etienne Marcel, provost of Paris, was the first to settle the city government in a town hall on Place de Greve, buying a two-storeyed house from the king on behalf of the city in 1357. Known as La Maison des Piliers for its row of arcades, it was eventually replaced by a magnificent Renaissance building begun under Francois I.

The Ile Saint-Louis was developed in the first half of the 17th century, transforming two muddy islands — l'Ile Notre-Dame and l'Ile aux Vaches — into the elegant residential quarter you see today. Corneille marvelled at how 'a whole city had sprung from an old ditch.'

The Marquis de Sade was transferred to the Bastille from Vincennes in 1784. He fashioned a megaphone from a funnel and shouted to passersby that prisoners were being murdered inside. The authorities removed him in early July 1789 — just days before the storming. At the Bastille he wrote some of his most notorious works, including Justine.

When Prince Czartoryski bought the Hotel Lambert, it became the centre of Polish exile in Paris. Chopin performed in its salons, and the poet Adam Mickiewicz was a frequent guest. A museum of Polish history was established here, preserving the memory of a nation that had lost its independence.

In 1763-64, the seven-year-old Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart stayed at the Hotel de Beauvais during his first visit to Paris. From here, the child prodigy was introduced to the court at Versailles, where he astonished Louis XV and his family with his extraordinary musical gifts.

Contemporary accounts described the Hotel-Dieu's wards as containing 'the ill, the dying and the dead' sharing the same beds. Philippe-Auguste donated the straw from his royal horses to serve as bedding. The stench was so overwhelming that visitors could smell the hospital from across the river.

Madame de Sevigne, the great epistolary writer, was married here on 4 August 1644 — at two o'clock in the morning. The peculiar hour was typical of aristocratic weddings of the period, designed to avoid crowds and spectacle.

After the Commune burned the original Hotel de Ville in 1871, the Third Republic rebuilt it with lavish interiors designed to project the permanence and grandeur of the new regime. Inside you'll find a bust by Rodin and magnificent murals by Puvis de Chavannes — some of the finest civic decorations in Paris.

Henri IV dreamed of transforming this area with a monumental Place de France — a grand new gateway to Paris from the east, with majestic avenues named after the kingdom's provinces fanning outward, and a canal running north from the Seine to lend a Venetian touch. But the concept died with the King, assassinated on 14 May 1610. Today only the shabby rues de Poitou, Bretagne and Normandie, and the curved rue Debelleyme that links them, survive as the ghostly trace of that magnificent unrealised project.

The Marché des Enfants Rouges is the oldest covered market in Paris, named after the orphans who once lived at 90 rue des Archives, dressed in red — the colour of Christian charity. Their female counterparts wore blue and were known as 'les enfants bleus.' The market narrowly escaped demolition: at the time Thirza Vallois was writing her guide, it had been earmarked for replacement by a modern block and a car park. Mercifully, public outcry saved it, and today it thrives as one of the most beloved food markets in the Marais.

Place de Greve was where people gathered in early morning to seek work, a practice called 'faire la greve.' The expression survives in modern French but now means 'to go on strike' — the opposite of its original meaning of seeking employment.

André Malraux's heritage law of 4 August 1962 saved this mansion — and the entire Marais — from demolition. The Revolution had left the Hôtel Salé disfigured beyond recognition. The City of Paris bought it in 1962 and leased it to the state. After Picasso's death in 1973, his heirs donated not only his own works but paintings from his private collection by Renoir, Cézanne, Douanier Rousseau, Matisse and Braque — transforming a rescued ruin into one of the world's great museums of modern art.

La Voisin's trial in 1680 at the Arsenal was another memorable event. Women of distinction, taking the Marquise de Brinvilliers as a model, set out to eliminate those they found cumbersome. So many names of high-ranking ladies leaked out that procedures were hastened to silence her.

The church is named after Saint Mederic, a 7th-century abbot whose remains were said to scintillate with miraculous light. His cult drew pilgrims to this spot for centuries, and local legends attributed healing powers to his relics.

On Friday 17 July 1676, Madame de Sevigne watched the Marquise de Brinvilliers carried to Place de Greve. The Marquise had poisoned her father (requiring ten attempts) and two brothers. Her lover Godin de Sainte-Croix had learned the art of poison from an Italian named Exili while imprisoned in the Bastille. Sevigne wrote: 'At last, it is all over, the Brinvilliers is in the air.'

During the Paris Commune in May 1871, Communards attempted to burn Notre-Dame by piling chairs and furniture against the doors and setting them alight. Doctors and staff from the neighbouring Hotel-Dieu rushed across and extinguished the flames, saving the cathedral from destruction.

The church of Saint-Louis-en-l'Ile was designed by Louis Le Vau, the same architect who created the Hotel Lambert just down the street. Its most distinctive feature is the unusual openwork iron spire, quite unlike any other church tower in Paris. The nearby Hotel du Jeu de Paume recalls the island's quieter days.

The Hotel Chalons de Luxembourg is distinguished by its magnificent lion's head portal. The Italian poet and adventurer Gabriele d'Annunzio lived here in 1914, during his flamboyant Parisian exile before returning to Italy to agitate for entry into the Great War.

In 1118, the brilliant philosopher Peter Abelard came to this street to tutor the young Heloise, niece of Canon Fulbert. Their passionate love affair — one of the most famous in history — ended in catastrophe when Fulbert, enraged by a secret marriage and pregnancy, hired thugs to castrate Abelard. Heloise became a nun, Abelard a monk, and their anguished love letters became classics of medieval literature.

The 28 statues of the Kings of Judah on the west facade were torn down by Revolutionaries who mistook them for the Kings of France. The heads were discovered in 1977 during construction work near the Opera and are now displayed at the Musee de Cluny.

This corner table — yes, this exact one — is where Sartre scribbled Being and Nothingness while chain-smoking Gauloises. De Beauvoir sat across from him, writing her own masterpiece. The hot chocolate recipe hasn't changed since 1887.

Between 1163 and 1330, anonymous artisans carved Notre-Dame from stone, slipping imperceptibly from the Romanesque to the Gothic style yet sustaining architectural unity. Bishop Maurice de Sully initiated the project, commissioning a monument to transcend every other in the kingdom.

On the wall of the school on rue des Rosiers, an inscription reads 'N'OUBLIEZ PAS' — Do Not Forget. It commemorates the 165 Jewish pupils who were deported from this school during the Occupation and murdered in the death camps. None survived.

The presence of royalty in the Marais ended brutally on 30 June 1559, when Henri II was fatally wounded during a friendly tournament in the gardens of the Hôtel des Tournelles — the site on which this square now stands. His opponent, the Comte de Montgomery, captain of the Scottish guard, shattered a lance that pierced the King's eye. Henri lingered for ten agonising days before dying on 10 July. His bereaved wife Catherine de Medici abandoned the accursed place at once, eventually settling at the newly built Palais des Tuileries. In 1565 she ordered the Hôtel des Tournelles razed to the ground, to blot it from her memory — inadvertently clearing the ground for Henri IV's masterpiece.

The priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs traces its origins to the 6th century, when a primitive oratory stood on the Ile de la Cite. In the 8th century a chapel replaced it north of the island, but the Normans tore it down a century later. The priory as a fortified complex wasn't built until the 12th century, situated outside the city walls. The monks played a major role in developing this part of Paris, and gave the kingdom renowned churchmen — notably Cardinal de Richelieu. It all came to an end with the Revolution, and in 1798 the newly founded Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers was granted the premises.

Rue Saint-Martin lies on the ancient Roman road from Lutetia to the north, a continuation of the Roman cardo — the main urban street — which runs as rue Saint-Jacques south of the Seine. For centuries the Porte Saint-Martin was the ceremonial entry point to Paris.

The Pont-Marie is named not for the Virgin Mary or Marie de Medici, as many assume, but for Christophe Marie, the entrepreneur who developed the Ile Saint-Louis in the 17th century. A statue of Sainte Genevieve, patroness of Paris, watches over the bridge.

At 56 rue de Turenne, a plain house with a modest statue of the Virgin marks the former home of the burlesque writer Scarron and his fifteen-year-old bride Françoise d'Aubigné — an ill-matched couple if ever there was one. Scarron was deformed, crippled, and twenty-six years her elder; but an impoverished orphan's only choices were marriage or a nunnery. At night he screamed in pain that even opium could not relieve; by day he hid his suffering under sallies and laughs. Writers and noblemen climbed to his second-floor room to enjoy his company, drawing chairs around a four-poster bed covered in yellow damask. Scarron died here in 1660, leaving debts and a new literary genre. His practical young widow rose from governess to official mistress to wife of Louis XIV himself — Madame de Maintenon, the only woman in French history to make that ascent.

On 13 August 1792, a sumptuous dinner was served in the drawing-room of the Temple — the same room where Mozart had once played the harpsichord. The guests were the Royal Family, virtually prisoners of the Commune of Paris. The King was addressed merely as 'Monsieur' and treated with a courtesy that was entirely sham: as soon as dinner ended, the royal couple, their two children and the King's sister were locked in the Tower of the Temple. Louis XVI was held here until his execution on 21 January 1793. The Queen followed him to the Conciergerie the next summer. Their seven-year-old son, the Dauphin, was torn from his family and left to rot in a dark cell until his presumed death on 8 June 1795. When the body was exhumed in 1894, the bones proved to belong to an 18-year-old youth — and the mystery of the lost Dauphin has never been resolved. Napoleon prudently razed the Tower to the ground, but not before some forty pretenders had claimed the throne.

Madame de Sévigné, born in 1626 on Place Royale — now Place des Vosges — lost her father in childhood and both her mother and grandparents by the age of ten. Constantly on the move through nine different homes in the Marais, she finally found her permanent home here at Hôtel Carnavalet in 1677. 'Thank God, we have it,' she wrote to her beloved daughter. 'It is an admirable affair — we shall have a beautiful courtyard, a beautiful garden, a beautiful neighbourhood.' She lived here for the last twenty years of her life, devouring books, observing the world around her and writing the extraordinary letters to her daughter that became an invaluable testimony of 17th-century Paris. Eight tapestries of Noah and seven of Psyche hung on her walls. The city purchased the Hôtel in 1866 and turned it into the museum of the history of Paris.

The priory had a darker side. Its gaol was the scene of a savage massacre during the Hundred Years' War, when the Bourguignons slaughtered their Armagnac rivals within these walls. Under Louis XIV, prostitutes captured on the neighbouring streets were kept here awaiting deportation to New Orleans. In September 1719, 180 male prisoners were brought from the prison of Bicetre, to be married to 180 women. The couples were then chained together and marched all the way to La Rochelle on the Atlantic coast, where they embarked for Louisiana — a forced marriage and forced migration in one brutal stroke.

The church takes its name from the white-robed begging friars who arrived from Marseilles in 1258, seeking alms in the neighbourhood. When Saint Louis suppressed mendicant orders, they were replaced by the black-gowned Guillemites — yet the name 'Blancs-Manteaux' (white cloaks) stuck, a ghostly reminder of those original penitents. Sartre later commemorated the street in a poem.

These two half-timbered houses on rue Francois-Miron are the only ones in Paris securely dated to the 14th century. Their steep gabled roofs are a rare survival of medieval Paris. At number 4, the Couperin family of musicians lived for generations — a dynasty that dominated French keyboard music for nearly two centuries.

The Arsenal houses the apartment of Madame de Meilleraye, a unique surviving example of a Louis XIII interior. The Marechal de Meilleraye commissioned Simon Vouet to create a dwelling of great splendour for his young bride.

In 1290, a Jew named Jonathas was accused of host desecration — stabbing a consecrated wafer that allegedly bled. He was burned at the stake and a chapel was erected on the site to commemorate the supposed miracle. This was one of many such blood libels that fuelled antisemitic violence across medieval Europe.

The Hotel d'Aumont represents a collaboration between three of the greatest names in 17th-century French art. Louis Le Vau designed it for the playwright Scarron, then Francois Mansart remodelled it for the Duc d'Aumont, and Charles Le Brun painted the magnificent ceiling — a concentration of genius unmatched in any other private mansion in the Marais.

During the Revolution, Notre-Dame was nearly lost forever. Stripped of its treasures and rededicated to the Cult of Reason, it was put up for sale as building material. A certain Citoyen Simon nearly purchased the cathedral — one of the closest brushes with destruction in the building's history.

The present Hôtel de Soubise rose from the ruins of the Hôtel de Guise in 1705, built by the architect Delamair for the House of Rohan-Soubise. Its first proprietress, Anne de Rohan, had yielded her charms to Louis XIV, who gratefully financed the construction — a situation her cuckolded husband chose to ignore. Wagging tongues said that while 'Louis XIV had supplied the wood' — a pun, since 'bois' also means antler, as in a cuckold's horns — 'his friends threw in the stones.' Today the entire history of France is packed into 200 kilometres of archival shelves, while wall paintings by Boucher and Van Loo give the visitor an idea of aristocratic taste in the first half of the 18th century. The spectacular colonnade courtyard is unique in Paris, and Delamair preserved the two medieval Gothic turrets at a time when such architecture was held in contempt.

Place de Greve served as Paris's main place of public executions, with gallows as a permanent fixture. Notable executions included Cartouche, the terror of early 18th-century Paris; Ravaillac, assassin of Henri IV; and the Marquise de Brinvilliers, mass poisoner.

The Ile Saint-Louis was originally two separate islands: l'Ile Notre-Dame, serving as the cathedral's recreational grounds, and l'Ile aux Vaches, the domain of grazing cows, laundresses and lovers. During the 14th century, a defence tower with a moat divided them. In the first half of the 17th century, the moat was filled in and the two islands united into the Ile Saint-Louis.

The Hotel Lambert is considered Louis Le Vau's masterpiece of domestic architecture. Built for Lambert de Thorigny, it features a celebrated rotunda balcony that projects over the Seine. Prince Adam Czartoryski purchased it in 1843 and the Rothschild family acquired it in 1975.

Constantin Brancusi bequeathed his entire studio to the French state on condition it be preserved exactly as he left it. The recreated atelier beside the Pompidou contains his tools, unfinished works, and personal effects. Man Ray's widow fought tenaciously for the studio's preservation, ensuring that one of the 20th century's most important sculptors would be remembered in situ.

The remains of Abelard and Heloise have had an extraordinary journey through the centuries. They were reunited in death and now lie together at Pere Lachaise cemetery — the most visited grave in that famous necropolis. Medallion portraits of the lovers can be seen at 9 quai aux Fleurs, near the site of their fateful encounter.

The Val-de-Grace is one of the most important religious monuments of seventeenth-century France, and the only one in Paris preserved entirely intact. Every other great church of that century in the capital has been damaged, rebuilt, or stripped of its surroundings in some way. Here the chapel, the cloister, and the garden a la francaise stand together as they were meant to stand, restored in recent decades and separated from the hospital wards that grew up around them. You are looking at the last complete Grand Siecle religious ensemble in the city.

script_body: This abbey began as a desperate bargain with God. Anne of Austria was thirty-six years old and still childless when she vowed to build a temple if she were granted an heir. A year later, in 1638, a first son was born, the future Louis XIV. When he reached the age of reason in 1645, the Queen brought the boy king here herself to lay the cornerstone of the royal abbey she had promised. The Val-de-Grace is, in a very literal sense, the debt his mother paid for his birth.

Louis XIV was born in 1638, a year after the vow
In 1645 at his age of reason, Louis XIV laid the cornerstone
source_passage: the 36-year-old childless Anne of Austria vowed to build a temple to God should she be granted an heir

script_body: The abbey became one of the finest examples of 17th-century French architecture, designed by Francois Mansart and Lemercier. Both architects took particular pride in its graceful dome — the feature they considered their triumph here. You can still read that pride in the dome overhead: a balance of weight and lift that was meant, from the beginning, to be the thing you notice first.

script_body: Inside the dome, Mignard painted an astounding mural depicting two hundred figures — among them Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, the couple whose childless years and eventual heir made this building possible in the first place. The mural is to the glory of God, but it is also, very deliberately, to the glory of the family that built the church. Two hundred painted figures, and the two whose vow started everything are among them.

script_body: In 1793 the Convention decided to convert the abbey into a hospital and a medical school for the army. The decision came into effect three years later, in 1796. In 1852 Napoleon III added a medical library to the school, and by then the collection already held 130,000 theses and 4,000 other works. Expansion was inevitable, and the buildings suffered much damage as the medical institution grew around the old royal church.

script_body: In 1978 a happier initiative was taken: to restore the old monument and separate its activities from the rest of the hospital. The chapel, the cloister and the garden a la francaise have already been restored. By 1996, in time for the bicentennial, the project is to be completed with the addition of a museum of the army's health service — an institution that was born here during the Revolution coming home, in effect, to the building that first housed it.

script_body: In 1685, Guillaume Brice wrote what is called the first guidebook to Paris, and he singled this place out. Foreigners, he argued, must agree that things in France can be made beautiful and regular like those one goes to admire in Italy. It is a quiet boast — and a revealing one. At a moment when educated Europe still looked to Rome and Florence for the standard of architectural beauty, the first Parisian guidebook writer pointed his readers here, to the Val-de-Grace, to make the case that France could do the same.

If it's cold, step into Café Ma Bourgogne at the northwest corner; the view of the square is nearly as good from the window.

script_body: Walk up rue de Birague — stop and look at the shops — and continue into the place des Vosges. Henri IV himself planned that visiting dignitaries would enter the square exactly this way, through the rue de Birague gate.

[...] it was Henri's intention that all visiting foreign dignitaries arriving in Paris would enter by the gate just to the east of here, at the Bastille, travel down the rue Saint-Antoine, and then turn into the place Royale from what is now the rue de Birague, where you entered.

script_body: Victor Hugo put it bluntly: "It's the blow of Montgomery's lance that created the place des Vosges." In 1559 a royal palace called Tournelles stood on this ground, and Henri II, having already won two jousts that day, insisted on a third against the captain of his Scottish Guards, Gabriel de Lorges, sire de Montgomery. Montgomery was reluctant. The king, savoring his success, had his way. At the second pass Montgomery's lance broke, and by a freak accident the point pushed up the visor of the king's helmet and entered his head above his eye. For ten days Henri suffered. The greatest doctors were called; Ambroise Paré and Andreas Vesalius came all the way from Brussels. Four criminals under sentence of death were decapitated so that the doctors could study their cranial anatomy, but to no avail. Henri died — of infection if nothing else — and his widow Catherine de Médicis persuaded her son Charles IX to demolish the palace with its unhappy memories.

physical_cues.cue: The ground of the place des Vosges — where the Tournelles palace stood until Charles IX had it demolished after Henri II's death

source_passage: C'est le coup de lance de Montgomery qui a créé la place des Vosges. —Victor Hugo. [...] It remained the royal residence until 1559 and the joust that cost Henri II his life. The king had fought and won two jousts already that day, but he insisted on a third against the captain of his Scottish Guards, Gabriel de Lorges, sire de Montgomery. At the first pass, both combatants splintered their lances. The king wanted another run; Montgomery was reluctant. Of course, the king, savoring his success, had his way. Once again Montgomery's lance broke, but this time, by a freak accident, the point pushed up the visor of the king's helmet and entered his head above his eye. For ten days Henri suffered. The greatest doctors were called; Ambroise Paré and Andreas Vesalius came all the way from Brussels. Four criminals under sentence of death were decapitated so that the doctors could study their cranial anatomy, but to no avail. Henri died, of infection if nothing else, and his widow, Catherine de Médicis, persuaded her son Charles IX to demolish the palace with its unhappy memories.

script_body: After royalty abandoned the Tournelles palace, the ground was used by the militia for exercises, by the city for stables and a powder store, and for a long time by a horse market that attracted rogues. Henri IV found the answer: replace the market with Paris's first real urban development project. Parceling began in 1605. He reserved the south side for himself, the north for a silk factory à la façon de Milan, and sold the east and west to private owners. The Duc de Sully filled half of his side with friends; the Duc de Guise did likewise. The king, a recent convert to Catholicism, was pleased: the new square housed Protestants and Catholics side by side.

physical_cues.cue: Pavillon du Roi at the south end of the square — the first building finished when parceling began in 1605

source_passage: Once royalty abandoned the palace, the ground on which it had stood was given over to a succession of improvised roles. The militia used it for its exercises. The city installed stables and used some of the buildings to store powder. [...] The answer was found by Henri IV. The horse market would be replaced by a development project, Paris's first. It would be a spacious, symmetrical public square to be known as the place Royale, a place of respectable residence and assembly. The parceling of terrain began in 1605 [...]. The Duc de Sully filled 50 percent of the pavilions with his friends. The Duc de Guise did likewise. The result was one that pleased Henri, a convert to Catholicism: a mix of Protestants and Catholics.

source_attribution.author: Sonia Landes, Alison Landes, Rebecca Landes

script_body: The façades were meant to be uniform: brick with pierre taillé — cut-stone — trim, two floors above four arcades of shops, capped by a steep slate roof pierced with mansard windows. The style was called bleu, blanc, rouge, for the slate roofs, the white stone trim, and the red bricks. In practice, only the first structures — the Pavillon du Roi among them — lived up to the plan. Brick was slow to lay and expensive, local workers lacked the skills, and Henri was in a hurry. Most later owners simply built in plaster on wood framing and painted them to resemble brick, in colors from dusty pink to dark red. Much of this trompe l'oeil is still visible around you. These masterpieces of French architecture, praised for their proportions and colors, were mostly façade.

Steep slate roofs with mansard windows
Four-arcade covered walkways at ground level

inline_foreign_phrases.gloss: blue, white, red — for the slate roofs, white stone trim, and red bricks

source_passage: The facades were to be all the same, built of brick with pierre taillé (cut-stone) trim. The ground floor, planned for shops, was set back to create a covered walkway of four arcades per lot: each building was to have two floors above that, the whole capped with a steep slate roof encompassing another two floors pierced with mansard windows. The style was known as bleu, blanc, rouge—for the slate roofs, the white stone trim, and the red bricks. [...] In principle, the buildings around the square were to be made of brick with stone trim. In fact, only the first structures, including the Pavillon du Roi, lived up to the plan. [...] the owners of the later buildings were only too happy to construct them of plaster on wood framing and then paint them to resemble brick, in colors ranging from dusty pink to dark red. Some of this trompe l'oeil is still visible. It is surprising that these masterpieces of French architecture—praised for their concept, size, proportions, and colors—were mostly facade.

source_attribution.author: Sonia Landes, Alison Landes, Rebecca Landes

script_body: Henri IV was assassinated shortly before the square was finished, and so it was inaugurated by his son, the young Louis XIII — which is why the equestrian statue in the center of the square is of Louis XIII, not of Henri IV. The inauguration, on April 5, 6, and 7 of 1612, was a three-day spectacle. Jousting was forbidden now, but five equestrian ballets were staged for the cavaliers, each in different exotic costumes — one group dressed as American Indians. One quadrille alone involved the Duc de Longueville and his retainers in gray-violet satin with silver embroidery, their pages and horses in red velvet, four winged horses pulling a chariot with two rhinoceroses harnessed behind, and two blue-satin giants preceding the duke himself on a horse draped in repoussé silver and gold. There were one hundred and fifty musicians, continuous parades, fireworks at night, and ten thousand spectators. Members of the royal entourage had been assigned specific houses and balconies — and for the first time, Paris houses had been built with real balconies instead of the thin stone ledges Parisians had leaned on before. Once the place Royale had shown the way, balconies became de rigueur. The common people had to hang from chimneys or squeeze into the arcades. Of one delegation of ambassadors Mme de Motteville wrote: "In general they are so fat that they give you heartburn, and concerning their bodies, they are dirty."

physical_cues.cue: Wrought-iron balconies along the façades on every side of the square
Equestrian statue of Louis XIII in the center of the square

source_passage: Unfortunately, Henri IV was assassinated shortly before the square's completion. The square was therefore inaugurated by the young Louis XIII. This is why the equestrian statue in the center of the square is of Louis XIII, and not of Henri IV. On April 5, 6, and 7, 1612, a fabulous tournament was held at the resplendent place Royale. Jousting was forbidden, but five equestrian ballets were organized for the cavaliers, each with different exotic costumes—including one group dressed as American Indians. [...] the Duc de Longueville and his retainers were dressed in gray violet satin with silver embroidery; the pages and the horses were dressed in red velvet; four winged horses pulled a chariot with two rhinoceroses harnessed to the back; and two giants in blue satin preceded the duke himself, who rode a horse draped with repoussé plaques of silver and gold. There were one hundred and fifty musicians, as well as games, continuous parades, and fireworks at night. The square was packed with ten thousand people [...]. It was the first time that houses had been built with real balconies; until then Parisians had had only small stone ledges to lean on. Once the place Royale had shown the way, balconies quickly became de rigueur. The common people had to hang from the chimneys or squeeze into the recesses of the arcades. [...] Of one delegation Mme de Motteville wrote, after describing their rich clothes studded with jewels, 'In general they are so fat that they give you heartburn, and concerning their bodies, they are dirty.'

source_attribution.author: Sonia Landes, Alison Landes, Rebecca Landes

script_body: The place Royale was the favourite dueling ground of the French aristocracy; fashionable ladies of the square enjoyed the spectacle, and swordsmen were encouraged by these admirers. In 1614 three out of four antagonists were killed in a single encounter. In 1626 Cardinal Richelieu, first minister of Louis XIII, forbade dueling on pain of death. The ban itself was the challenge: a year later, a six-man duel — two principals and four seconds, who were expected to do more than hold the combatants' coats — took place right in front of the Pavillon du Roi. Two dead, two fled to England, two off to Lorraine. The latter two were caught en route, brought back to Paris, and decapitated, over the protests of the nobility of France. Richelieu was not a man to take insolence lightly. In 1643, after his death, the last scion of the Protestant Colignys dueled with Henri, Duc de Guise — grandson of the man who had killed Coligny's grandfather, Admiral Coligny, in the 1572 Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre. Guise was wounded first, but managed to grab Coligny's épée, hold it, and simply finish him off. The king, hoping to end the enmity between Catholics and Protestants, chose not to punish the victor.

physical_cues.cue: Pavillon du Roi — the central pavilion on the south side

source_passage: The place Royale was also the favorite dueling ground for the hotbloods of the French aristocracy. [...] In 1614, three out of four antagonists were killed in one encounter [...]. In 1626, Richelieu, first minister of Louis XIII, forbade dueling on pain of death. [...] Only one year later there occurred a six-man duel (two principals and four seconds, who were expected to do more than hold the combatants' coats) right in front of the Pavillon du Roi. Results: two dead, two fled to England, and two off to Lorraine. The latter two were caught en route, brought back to Paris, and decapitated, over the protests and appeals of the nobility of France. Richelieu was not a man to take insolence lightly. [...] In 1643, after Richelieu's death, the last scion of the Protestant Colignys dueled with Henri, Duc de Guise, grandson of the man who had killed Coligny's grandfather, Admiral Coligny, in the aftermath of the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre, the slaughter of the Protestants during the religious wars (1572). [...] Guise was wounded first, but managed to grab Coligny's épée (sword), hold it, and simply finish him off. This time the king, hoping to end the enmity between Catholics and Protestants, chose not to punish the victor.

script_body: Not all the action in the square was outdoors. The place Royale became the centre of Parisian social life, and fashionable ladies of the neighbourhood — Ninon de Lenclos and Marion Delorme among them — invented a new and durable institution. They met at intimate gatherings called ruelles, at which the elegant guests rivaled one another in wit, fine speech, and social finesse. Molière parodied their excesses in his play Les Précieuses Ridicules. The gatherings took place in the hostesses' bedrooms, perhaps because an amazing number of the hostesses were as renowned for their sexual prowess as their social. Several of the great ladies of the place Royale could hardly keep track of their lovers.

script_body: During the Revolution the place Royale was renamed the place de l'Indivisibilité, after the new Republic, one and indivisible. Then, in 1800, the name was changed again — to place des Vosges, to honour the first French département to pay its taxes that year. Lovers of old Paris still argue for the return of the original name.

script_body: The garden is the subject of an ongoing argument: keep the trees, or cut them down. The large leafy trees you see were not here originally, and for good reason — they block the view of the place. The French have always been devoted to vistas, which is one reason why Paris is such a beautiful city. The original garden was minimal: lawns with paths cut on the diagonal, leaving an unobstructed view of the whole square. The trees standing here today are the second set; the first, a ring around the statue, were struck down by Dutch elm disease. From a second-floor window of the Musée Victor Hugo you can see how magnificent the whole square looks when it's uninterrupted by trees — and you too may side with the preservationists.

physical_cues.cue: Large leafy trees in the central garden, obstructing the view across the square

source_passage: The garden before you is the subject of great and ongoing controversy: to keep or not to keep the trees. To preservationists and purists, the large leafy trees are an intrusion. They weren't there originally, and for good reason: they block the view of the place. The French have always been devoted to vistas, which is one reason why Paris is such a beautiful city. [...] the original garden was minimal—lawns with paths cut on the diagonal—in order to leave an unobstructed view of the whole square. The trees that are here today are the second set of trees to be planted in the garden. The circle of trees that had surrounded the statue were stricken with dutch elm disease and were replaced. [...] When you visit the Musée Victor Hugo, look out of the windows from the second story onto the place. You will be astounded to see how magnificent the whole square looks when it is uninterrupted by the trees. You too may be tempted to side with the historical preservationists.

source_attribution.author: Sonia Landes, Alison Landes, Rebecca Landes

script_body: Beginning in the eighteenth century the Marais went into a long decline. The aristocracy moved west to the Faubourg Saint-Honoré, where the Palais Elysée and the British and American embassies stand today — in part because the prevailing winds from the west carried the unpleasant odours of central Paris away from the new districts. The old palaces here were abandoned to manufacturing. Heavy machinery was bolted to parquet floors, reception rooms divided into two-storey workspaces, courtyards filled with sheds. If not for this industrial afterlife, the place des Vosges would not have survived — the factories kept the buildings heated and roofed. After World War II the trend reversed, and a 1962 law requiring the ravalement — the cleaning — of every Paris façade at least once a decade transformed the city. The Marais was one of the biggest winners: black and grey hôtels suddenly took on the colours and detail of their youth. Jacques Lang, the former minister of culture, was an early resident of the restored square.

physical_cues.cue: Restored red-brick façades, brighter where cleaning has been done

source_passage: Beginning in the eighteenth century, the Marais went into a decline. The center of Paris fashion and social activity moved steadily westward. The aristocracy moved to the Faubourg Saint-Honoré, where the Palais Elysée and the British and American embassies are now located [...]. The fashionable neighborhoods grew toward the west, in part because the prevailing winds came from the west and carried the unpleasant odors of central and eastern Paris away from the residents of these fine new neighborhoods. Palaces were abandoned to manufacturing and trade. Heavy machinery was bolted to elegant parquet floors [...]. If not for these enterprises, the place des Vosges would have disappeared. They kept the buildings heated, roofed, and occupied. [...] Serious renewal of the Marais came later, with a special push from the law of 1962 that required the cleaning (ravalement) of the facades of all buildings at least once every decade or so. [...] Jacques Lang, the former minister of culture, was an early resident of the restored place des Vosges.

source_attribution.author: Sonia Landes, Alison Landes, Rebecca Landes

script_body: The Pavillon du Roi at no. 1 — the central pavilion on the south side — was never occupied by the king himself. It was too small for him and his retinue; his concierge, the gatekeeper, was the first resident. Since 1666 it has been rented to different tenants, and today it is divided into apartments served by ugly stairs and an elevator crammed into the right-hand side of the central arcade — an eighteenth-century intrusion that still rankles, because it blocks part of the vista from the rue de Birague. As early as 1752 the writer Germain Brice argued that the three arcades of the pavilion should be torn down to leave the Louis XIII statue visible all the way from the rue Saint-Antoine: "It has to hurt," he wrote, "to see one of the three arcades blocked to make a nasty stairway… we have such little care for public embellishments in Paris." Look up, though: the balcony here is stone rather than wrought iron, and a bust of Henri IV watches the square from above. Walk through the arcade and, on the rue de Birague side, you'll see the king's arms and initials above the arches, still there from the original construction.

Stone balcony above the central arch, with a bust of Henri IV
Arms and initials of Henri IV above the arches, on the rue de Birague side
